```
You wrote "one micro-USB OTG port." The Pi Zero W actually has **two** micro-USB connectors: a power-only "PWR IN" jack and a data-capable "USB" jack (the only OTG-capable one). Only the "USB" jack should go to the target machine as the HID+storage gadget. **Power the Pi from the dedicated PWR IN jack** (wall adapter or powered hub), not parasitically from the target's USB port.
```

```json
  "content": "#!/bin/bash\n#\n# gadget-teardown.sh\n#\n# Cleanly tears down the composite gadget in the order configfs requires:\n# unbind the UDC first (drops the device from the host), then remove the\n# config symlinks, then the functions, then the now-empty directories.\n# Safe to run when nothing is set up -- every step is best-effort.\n\nGADGET_NAME=kvmdongle\nGADGET_DIR=/sys/kernel/config/usb_gadget/$GADGET_NAME\n\nif [ ! -d \"$GADGET_DIR\" ]; then\n    exit 0\nfi\n\ncd \"$GADGET_DIR\" || exit 0\n\necho \"\" > UDC 2>/dev/null || true\n\nrm -f configs/c.1/hid.usb0 2>/dev/null || true\nrm -f configs/c.1/hid.usb1 2>/dev/null || true\nrm -f configs/c.1/mass_storage.usb0 2>/dev/null || true\n\nrmdir functions/hid.usb0 2>/dev/null || true\nrmdir functions/hid.usb1 2>/dev/null || true\nrmdir functions/mass_storage.usb0 2>/dev/null || true\n\nrmdir configs/c.1/strings/0x409 2>/dev/null || true\nrmdir configs/c.1 2>/dev/null || true\nrmdir strings/0x409 2>/dev/null || true\n\ncd /\nrmdir \"$GADGET_DIR\" 2>/dev/null || true\n\nrm -f /run/kvmdongle/gadget-info.json 2>/dev/null || true\n\necho \"[gadget-teardown] done\"\n"
}
```

Picking up where the outage cut in: I'd finished writing all the code and was validating it. Here's where things stand.

**Validation done** (pygame has no prebuilt wheel yet for the Python 3.14 on this machine, and building from source failed, so I built a minimal fake-pygame stub in a local `.venv` to exercise the real logic instead of just eyeballing it):
- `protocol.py` — round-tripped every frame type, including byte-by-byte delivery and checksum-corruption resync. All passed.
- `pi/daemon.py` — tested keyboard report assembly (modifier bits, 6-key limit with correct drop-not-overwrite behavior), mouse report assembly (button state persisting across move-only reports, wide deltas splitting into multiple ≤127 reports), and the storage controller (path-traversal/nonexistent-file rejection, mount/eject actually writing the LUN attribute). All passed.
- `client.py` — imported it against the fake pygame to check the KEY_MAP/CHAR_MAP tables for typos or collisions, and drove the `MenuBar` class directly to confirm the new dynamic-Storage-menu mechanism (menus whose items depend on live Pi state) triggers `on_open` correctly and that per-row click handlers close over the right filename (the classic lambda late-binding bug). All passed.

Everything is written per the approved plan:

- **`protocol.py`** — shared, checksummed, bidirectional wire protocol
- **`client.py`** — laptop app, same UI/menu bar/hotkeys as the old Arduino version, plus bidirectional serial (reader thread + queue) and a new Storage menu for listing/mounting/ejecting ISOs
- **`pi/`** — `gadget-setup.sh`/`gadget-teardown.sh` (configfs composite gadget: HID keyboard + HID mouse + read-only CD-ROM), `daemon.py` (the control daemon), systemd units, `install.sh` (one-shot setup from a blank SD card), and the phase-2 Wi-Fi AP + upload page (`webui.py`, `hostapd.conf`/`dnsmasq.conf`, `wifi-ap-toggle.sh`, `install-webui.sh`)
- **`README.md`** — wiring, setup order, usage, power warning, troubleshooting
- **`.gitignore`** — excludes the local `.venv` I created for testing

Nothing here has touched real hardware yet — the next real test is running `pi/install.sh` on an actual Pi Zero W and `client.py` against it, per the Verification section in the plan. Let me know if you want me to walk through that bring-up with you when the hardware's in hand.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 12:52:29 AM</sup>

For the Pi Zero W (single-core ARM11), Raspberry Pi OS Lite really does boot slowly mostly because of everything it starts by default, not because of a desktop — you have three realistic options, in increasing order of effort:

- **DietPi** (recommended) — Debian-based, same `apt`/`systemd` foundation the whole `pi/` setup already assumes, with an official Zero W image. It ships almost nothing running by default, so boot is meaningfully faster out of the box. `install.sh`, the systemd units, and `wifi-ap-toggle.sh`'s `systemctl`/`NetworkManager` checks should carry over with little to no change.
- **Keep Raspberry Pi OS Lite, but trim it** — disable `triggerhappy`, `avahi-daemon`, `apt-daily`/`apt-daily-upgrade` timers, `dphys-swapfile`, `raspi-config`'s first-boot resize wait, and dhcpcd's network-wait-online, plus quiet boot params. Zero migration risk since it's the exact image already targeted, but won't beat DietPi's boot time.
- **Alpine or a custom Buildroot image** — the fastest possible boot, but Alpine uses OpenRC instead of systemd, which would mean rewriting every service file and every `systemctl`/`journalctl` call in `pi/` from scratch; Buildroot is a much bigger undertaking (custom kernel/rootfs build). Only worth it if boot time is a hard requirement beyond what DietPi gets you.

Want me to switch the Pi-side setup over to DietPi?

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 1:10:39 AM</sup>

All clear. Summary of the DietPi migration changes:

- **`pi/gadget-setup.sh`** — ISOs directory moved from `/home/pi/isos` to `/srv/kvmdongle/isos` (DietPi has no `pi` user by default; both `daemon.py` and `webui.py` already run as root, so a user-agnostic path made more sense anyway).
- **`pi/install.sh`** — same path change, dropped the now-pointless `chown pi:pi`, and generalized comments that named Raspberry Pi OS specifically.
- **`pi/wifi-ap-toggle.sh`** — DietPi doesn't run dhcpcd or NetworkManager by default, just plain `ifupdown`, so I added a third detection branch (`ifdown`/`ifup wlan0`) alongside the existing NetworkManager/dhcpcd cases. Caught a real bug while doing this: the original re-detected the network stack live when turning the AP back off, but by then the original stack had already been stopped/unmanaged, so it would misdetect and fail to restore it — fixed by recording the detected mode to `/run/kvmdongle/wifi-ap-prev-mode` when the AP goes on, and reading it back on off.
- **`README.md`** — swapped the setup instructions for DietPi's actual flow (correct ARMv6 image for the Zero W, `dietpi.txt` headless config, default `root`/`dietpi` login), updated the ISOs path, and noted the networking-stack auto-detection.

Everything else (`protocol.py`, `client.py`, `pi/daemon.py`, the systemd units, `config.txt`/`cmdline.txt` handling) is unaffected — DietPi is Debian+systemd like Raspberry Pi OS, so that layer carries over unchanged.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:09:48 AM</sup>

Yes, worth doing — this is exactly the kind of device that gets unplugged without a clean shutdown, and SD card corruption from unclean power loss is one of the most common Pi failure modes. The standard approach is an overlayfs-based read-only root (tmpfs absorbs writes, discarded on reboot) with `/srv/kvmdongle/isos` specifically excluded so it stays writable for uploads/SD swaps.

One wrinkle worth flagging: Raspberry Pi OS has a one-click "Overlay FS" toggle in `raspi-config`, but DietPi doesn't have as polished a built-in equivalent as far as I know — we'd likely be setting it up more manually (Debian's `overlayroot` package or a custom fstab/initramfs approach). Want me to look into the cleanest way to do that on DietPi specifically before I implement it?

```
# overlayRoot: Read-Only Root Filesystem with Overlay

## Core Functionality

overlayRoot implements a fail-safe read-only root filesystem by mounting the actual root at `/ro` and overlaying a temporary RAM disk (tmpfs) at `/rw`. This means all system modifications exist only in RAM and vanish on reboot unless explicitly persisted.

## Configuration & Installation

Installation involves cloning the repository and running `sudo bash install`, then customizing `/etc/overlayRoot.conf` to match your preferences. The script modifies your boot process by placing `init=/sbin/overlayRoot.sh` in `cmdline.txt`.

## Persistent Storage Strategy

To preserve data across reboots, add entries to `/etc/fstab` pointing to separate partitions or media. The documentation provides an example with UUID-based mounts for directories like `/mnt/root-rw`. The system explicitly rejects PARTUUIDs—you must use UUIDs instead, obtainable via the `blkid` command.
```

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:22:43 AM</sup>

Findings, confirmed via research: **DietPi has no built-in read-only-root toggle** — unlike Raspberry Pi OS's one-click `raspi-config` overlay option, DietPi requires a manual setup, using either the generic Debian `overlayroot` package or the Pi-specific `marklister/overlayRoot` script (both do the same thing: real root mounted at `/ro`, a tmpfs overlay on top for `/`, so any write just evaporates on reboot).

That surfaces a real structural snag for this project specifically: **whatever we use, `/srv/kvmdongle/isos` can't be part of that read-only overlay** — uploaded/copied ISOs need to actually survive a reboot, not vanish like every other write would. Normally you'd point a writable path like that at a separate USB drive, but the Zero W only has one data-capable USB port and it's already committed to the HID+storage gadget cable to the target. So the only way to get a genuinely persistent, writable ISOs folder alongside a read-only root is a **second partition on the same SD card**, carved out by shrinking the root filesystem — a one-time repartitioning step that carries its own (small but real) risk if it's interrupted.

Given that, there are two reasonable paths, and I'd rather you pick before I touch partitioning:

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:29:13 AM</sup>

Done. Summary of what's in place now:

**New files:**
- `pi/kvmdongle-storage-tune.service` — remounts root `noatime` on every boot (no fstab edits, so zero risk of a broken boot-critical file)
- `pi/journald-volatile.conf` — journal lives in RAM only, capped at 20MB (Zero W has just 512MB total)

**Changed:**
- `pi/install.sh` — installs both of the above, disables swap defensively, creates `/srv/kvmdongle/tmp`
- `pi/gadget-setup.sh` — now also writes `tmp_dir` into `gadget-info.json`
- `pi/webui.py` — points Python's `tempfile` module at that disk-backed `tmp_dir` explicitly
- `README.md` — documents the tradeoff and what was skipped

One thing worth calling out: I deliberately did **not** enable systemd's `tmp.mount` (tmpfs `/tmp`), even though it's a very standard part of this kind of hardening. Werkzeug (Flask's underlying library) spools large multipart uploads — i.e., a multi-GB ISO via the phase-2 web upload — through Python's default temp directory *before* `webui.py`'s code ever runs. If that directory were RAM-backed on a 512MB Zero W, a big enough upload could exhaust memory and crash the device. So `/tmp` stays disk-backed, and I pointed `tempfile.tempdir` at `/srv/kvmdongle/tmp` explicitly so this stays safe regardless.

This is the lightweight option — root isn't immune to corruption, just far less exposed, since routine writes are now rare. The full read-only-root path (via `overlayroot` + a second SD-card partition for the ISOs folder) is still there if you want it later.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:34:18 AM</sup>

Confirmed — here are both answers:

**Re-running `install.sh`**: Safe. Every step is idempotent — boot-config lines are only appended if missing, `cmdline.txt` editing only fires if a console entry is still there, `mkdir -p` never touches existing ISOs, and `systemctl enable`/`disable`/copy-file operations are all no-ops or harmless overwrites if already done. No data loss, no disruption to a running session.

That said, re-running the **current** `install.sh` won't actually add full read-only root — that feature doesn't exist yet (you picked the lightweight noatime/volatile-journal approach, remember). If you want the full version later, I'd build it as a **separate** script rather than folding it into `install.sh`, specifically because it involves repartitioning the SD card — that should be a deliberate one-time action you run once, not something that could accidentally fire again on a routine re-install.

**Webui/hostapd auto-start**: No, neither starts at boot. In `install-webui.sh` (pi/install-webui.sh:26-27,37) `hostapd`, `dnsmasq`, and `kvmdongle-webui` are all explicitly `disable`d after being installed — they only start when you run `wifi-ap-toggle.sh on`, and `wifi-ap-toggle.sh off` stops all three again. That's intentional: the Zero W has one Wi-Fi radio, so AP mode is meant to be an occasional, deliberate switch, not something running by default.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:42:19 AM</sup>

Done. Added remote AP control end-to-end:

- **`protocol.py`** — three new laptop→Pi commands (`AP_ENABLE`, `AP_DISABLE`, `AP_STATUS_QUERY`) and one Pi→laptop reply (`AP_STATUS`, carrying a bool).
- **`pi/daemon.py`** — new `WifiApController` class that shells out to `wifi-ap-toggle.sh` (whichever copy sits next to `daemon.py` in `/opt/kvmdongle/`) and checks `systemctl is-active hostapd` for real status rather than guessing. Replies with a clear error if phase 2 (`install-webui.sh`) was never installed, if the script exits non-zero, or if it times out (30s cap).
- **`client.py`** — new **Network** menu next to Storage: live "AP status: ON/OFF/unknown" line, Enable/Disable actions with a busy-state guard (same pattern as ISO mount/eject, so rapid clicks can't stack conflicting toggles). While fixing this I caught a real bug: the existing `ERROR` handler always cleared *storage* state regardless of which command actually failed — now that AP commands can also fail, it routes by the error's `failed_type` to the right state object instead.

Tested the new pieces directly (not just by reading): protocol round-trip for all four new frame types, and the daemon's `WifiApController` against a monkeypatched `subprocess.run` covering success, non-zero exit, and timeout — plus the missing-script case. All pass, and the full existing test suite (protocol/daemon/client keymap/menubar) still passes too.

One limitation worth knowing: the client only learns the AP's real state when it asks (opening the Network menu auto-queries, like Storage does) — it has no persistent memory of state from a previous session, so it shows "unknown" until the first query lands.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 2:32:42 PM</sup>

Done. The client window is now resizable (`pygame.RESIZABLE`), and I went with letterbox/pillarbox scaling rather than forcing the OS window itself into a locked aspect ratio — that approach is more robust across platforms and plays nicely with maximizing/tiling, whereas fighting the window manager to lock dimensions tends to get janky.

What changed in `client.py`:
- Window creation and the resize handler both pass `pygame.RESIZABLE`; a `VIDEORESIZE` event recreates the display surface at the new size (clamped to a sane minimum) and calls `menu.resize()` so the menu bar's background fill and right-aligned status text track the new width.
- Each frame now clears to black, computes the scale that fits the video into whatever space is left below the menu bar while preserving its native aspect ratio, and centers it — skipping the `smoothscale` call entirely when the size already matches (i.e., at native size, zero extra cost).
- Menu bar hit-testing is untouched by any of this — it draws unscaled in window-pixel space, and mouse-capture's relative deltas were already independent of window size.

Verified the scaling math directly (pillarbox case, letterbox case, exact-match no-op case, proportional shrink) since it's easy to get an off-by-one or divide-by-zero wrong there, plus re-ran the full existing test suite to confirm nothing else regressed.

140	## Adding more ISOs later (phase 2: Wi-Fi upload)
141	
142	The Pi Zero W's Wi-Fi radio can host a private AP with a small upload
143	page, so you don't need to pull the SD card each time. Since the Zero W
144	has only one radio, **AP mode and normal Wi-Fi networking aren't
145	concurrent** -- treat this as something you switch on only while
146	uploading, not an always-on mode. `wifi-ap-toggle.sh` detects whether
147	wlan0 is normally managed by NetworkManager, dhcpcd, or plain ifupdown
148	(DietPi's default) and restores whichever one it found when you turn the
149	AP back off.

153	cd KVMDongle/pi
154	sudo ./install-webui.sh
155	# then edit /opt/kvmdongle/hostapd.conf: change ssid and wpa_passphrase

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:00:48 PM</sup>

Both are real bugs I found and fixed, not just tuning:

**Grainy video above 1024x768** — two likely causes, both fixed:
1. **Windows DPI scaling**: `client.py` wasn't marked DPI-aware, so Windows was bitmap-stretching the whole window to match your display's scale factor (125%/150%, common on laptops) — invisible on chunky low-res content, glaringly obvious once there's fine text/detail. OBS declares DPI-awareness and never gets this treatment. Fixed with a `SetProcessDpiAwareness` call before any window is created.
2. **Capture format negotiation**: OpenCV's default Windows backend (Media Foundation) doesn't always negotiate the same mode as OBS with cheap UVC capture cards, and can fall back to a more compressed mode at higher resolutions. Switched to DirectShow (`cv2.CAP_DSHOW`), and added `--capture-width`/`--capture-height`/`--capture-fourcc` so you can force the exact mode OBS uses if DSHOW alone doesn't fully match it.

**Mouse lag** — found a real, concrete bug, not just latency tuning:
1. **Pi side**: `pi/daemon.py` was opening and closing `/dev/hidg1` on *every single HID report*. Opening a USB gadget character device isn't cheap, and mouse movement generates far more reports than keyboard input (worse still, a fast flick gets split into several reports, each with its own open/close). Now the fd is opened once at startup and kept open for the daemon's lifetime, unbuffered so writes still go out immediately.
2. **Laptop side**: the main loop called the capture device's blocking read directly, in the same loop that polls keyboard/mouse events — so any capture hiccup (common with USB capture dongles) delayed input forwarding by the same amount. Video capture now runs in its own background thread; the main loop just grabs the latest decoded frame and never blocks on it.

Verified the fix mechanically rather than just by inspection: a test with a simulated 200ms-per-frame capture device confirms `get_latest_frame()` still returns near-instantly, and the HID classes now hold a single injected fd for their whole lifetime with no re-opening logic left anywhere. Full existing test suite still passes.

"""
daemon.py

Runs on the Raspberry Pi as root (via kvmdongle-daemon.service, after
kvmdongle-gadget.service has brought up the USB gadget). Reads framed
commands off the GPIO UART control link from the laptop and:

  - translates KEY_DOWN/KEY_UP/MOUSE_* events into USB HID reports written
    to /dev/hidg0 (keyboard) and /dev/hidg1 (mouse), whose paths are read
    from /run/kvmdongle/gadget-info.json rather than hardcoded
  - handles LIST_ISOS / MOUNT_ISO / EJECT_ISO by scanning the ISOs
    directory and pointing the mass-storage function's LUN backing file
    at the requested ISO, replying with ACK/ERROR/ISO_LIST/etc.
  - handles AP_ENABLE / AP_DISABLE / AP_STATUS_QUERY by shelling out to
    wifi-ap-toggle.sh (phase 2, only present if install-webui.sh has been
    run), replying with the resulting AP_STATUS or an ERROR.

Single-threaded: the Pi Zero W is single-core, and every operation here
(HID writes, directory scans, LUN swaps) is fast enough that a plain
read-parse-handle loop introduces no meaningful latency. The AP toggle is
the one exception -- restarting hostapd/dnsmasq takes a few seconds, and
that blocks the loop for the duration, same trade-off already accepted
for ISO mount/eject. It's a rare, deliberate, user-initiated action, so a
few seconds of delayed key/mouse events (buffered by the OS, not lost) is
an acceptable cost.
"""

import json
import logging
import os
import signal
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import serial

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))
import protocol

GADGET_INFO_PATH = "/run/kvmdongle/gadget-info.json"
SERIAL_PORT = "/dev/serial0"
BAUD_RATE = 460800
MAX_HELD_KEYS = 6
EJECT_SETTLE_SECONDS = 0.3

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
)
log = logging.getLogger("kvmdongle-daemon")


def load_gadget_info(retries=50, delay=0.1):
    """Read the device paths written by gadget-setup.sh. Retries briefly in
    case of a startup race, even though systemd unit ordering should make
    this unnecessary."""
    last_err = None
    for _ in range(retries):
        try:
            with open(GADGET_INFO_PATH) as f:
                return json.load(f)
        except (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
            last_err = e
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not read {GADGET_INFO_PATH}: {last_err}")


class HidKeyboard:
    def __init__(self, fd, path):
        # fd is opened once, for the daemon's whole lifetime, with
        # buffering=0 (raw, unbuffered I/O) -- opening the HID gadget
        # character device is not cheap (the kernel function driver does
        # real setup work on every open()), and re-opening it for every
        # single report was adding significant, very noticeable latency to
        # mouse movement in particular, since a fast mouse flick can emit
        # several reports per event. path is kept only for logging.
        self.fd = fd
        self.path = path
        self.modifiers = 0
        self.held_keys = []  # ordered list of up to MAX_HELD_KEYS usage IDs

    def key_down(self, usage_id):
        if protocol.is_modifier_usage(usage_id):
            self.modifiers |= protocol.modifier_bit(usage_id)
        elif usage_id not in self.held_keys:
            if len(self.held_keys) < MAX_HELD_KEYS:
                self.held_keys.append(usage_id)
            else:
                log.debug("dropping key 0x%02X: 6 keys already held", usage_id)
        self._write_report()

    def key_up(self, usage_id):
        if protocol.is_modifier_usage(usage_id):
            self.modifiers &= ~protocol.modifier_bit(usage_id)
        elif usage_id in self.held_keys:
            self.held_keys.remove(usage_id)
        self._write_report()

    def release_all(self):
        self.modifiers = 0
        self.held_keys = []
        self._write_report()

    def _write_report(self):
        keys = self.held_keys + [0] * (MAX_HELD_KEYS - len(self.held_keys))
        report = bytes([self.modifiers & 0xFF, 0] + keys[:MAX_HELD_KEYS])
        _write_hid_report(self.fd, self.path, report)

    def close(self):
        try:
            self.fd.close()
        except OSError:
            pass


class HidMouse:
    def __init__(self, fd, path):
        self.fd = fd
        self.path = path
        self.buttons = 0

    def button_down(self, mask):
        self.buttons |= mask
        self._write_report(0, 0, 0)

    def button_up(self, mask):
        self.buttons &= ~mask
        self._write_report(0, 0, 0)

    def move(self, dx, dy):
        # HID report deltas are signed bytes (-127..127); split a wider
        # move into as many reports as needed.
        while dx != 0 or dy != 0:
            step_dx = max(-127, min(127, dx))
            step_dy = max(-127, min(127, dy))
            dx -= step_dx
            dy -= step_dy
            self._write_report(step_dx, step_dy, 0)

    def scroll(self, amount):
        self._write_report(0, 0, amount)

    def release_all_buttons(self):
        self.buttons = 0
        self._write_report(0, 0, 0)

    def _write_report(self, dx, dy, wheel):
        report = struct.pack("<Bbbb", self.buttons & 0xFF, dx, dy, wheel)
        _write_hid_report(self.fd, self.path, report)

    def close(self):
        try:
            self.fd.close()
        except OSError:
            pass


def _write_hid_report(fd, path, report_bytes):
    try:
        fd.write(report_bytes)
    except OSError as e:
        log.warning("failed to write HID report to %s: %s", path, e)


class StorageController:
    def __init__(self, lun_file_attr, isos_dir):
        self.lun_file_attr = lun_file_attr
        self.isos_dir = isos_dir
        self.current_iso = self._read_current_iso()

    def _read_current_iso(self):
        try:
            with open(self.lun_file_attr) as f:
                value = f.read().strip()
        except OSError:
            return None
        return os.path.basename(value) if value else None

    def list_isos(self):
        try:
            names = sorted(
                name for name in os.listdir(self.isos_dir)
                if name.lower().endswith(".iso")
            )
        except OSError as e:
            log.warning("could not list isos dir %s: %s", self.isos_dir, e)
            names = []
        return names, self.current_iso

    def mount(self, name):
        if "/" in name or "\\" in name or name in ("", ".", ".."):
            raise ValueError("invalid filename")
        path = os.path.join(self.isos_dir, name)
        if not os.path.isfile(path):
            raise ValueError(f"no such file: {name}")

        # Eject first, then insert, with a short settle delay so the host's
        # removable-media poll reliably observes both the "no medium" and
        # the "new medium" transitions rather than possibly missing one.
        self._write_lun("\n")
        time.sleep(EJECT_SETTLE_SECONDS)
        self._write_lun(path + "\n")
        self.current_iso = name

    def eject(self):
        self._write_lun("\n")
        self.current_iso = None

    def _write_lun(self, text):
        # A zero-byte write can be a no-op for some sysfs/configfs store
        # callbacks, so eject writes a bare newline rather than "".
        with open(self.lun_file_attr, "w") as f:
            f.write(text)


class WifiApController:
    """Shells out to wifi-ap-toggle.sh (phase 2, only present if
    install-webui.sh has been run on this Pi) to switch the ISO-upload
    Wi-Fi AP on/off, and asks systemd whether hostapd is currently active
    to report status."""

    TOGGLE_SCRIPT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "wifi-ap-toggle.sh")
    TOGGLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30

    def is_installed(self):
        return os.path.isfile(self.TOGGLE_SCRIPT)

    def is_enabled(self):
        try:
            result = subprocess.run(["systemctl", "is-active", "--quiet", "hostapd"], timeout=5)
        except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
            return False
        return result.returncode == 0

    def set_enabled(self, enabled):
        """Runs wifi-ap-toggle.sh on/off. Raises RuntimeError with a short
        message on failure (script missing, non-zero exit, or timeout)."""
        if not self.is_installed():
            raise RuntimeError("Wi-Fi AP not installed (run install-webui.sh on the Pi)")

        mode = "on" if enabled else "off"
        try:
            result = subprocess.run(
                [self.TOGGLE_SCRIPT, mode],
                capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=self.TOGGLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
            )
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            raise RuntimeError("timed out switching Wi-Fi AP mode")

        if result.returncode != 0:
            message = (result.stderr or result.stdout or "unknown error").strip()
            raise RuntimeError(message[:200])


class Daemon:
    def __init__(self):
        info = load_gadget_info()
        # buffering=0: raw, unbuffered binary I/O -- every .write() call is
        # an immediate syscall, with no Python-level buffer that could hold
        # a report back until it happens to fill up.
        keyboard_fd = open(info["hidg_keyboard"], "wb", buffering=0)
        mouse_fd = open(info["hidg_mouse"], "wb", buffering=0)
        self.keyboard = HidKeyboard(keyboard_fd, info["hidg_keyboard"])
        self.mouse = HidMouse(mouse_fd, info["hidg_mouse"])
        self.storage = StorageController(info["lun0_file_attr"], info["isos_dir"])
        self.wifi_ap = WifiApController()
        self.parser = protocol.FrameParser()
        self.ser = serial.Serial(SERIAL_PORT, BAUD_RATE, timeout=0.1, exclusive=True)
        self.running = True

    def run(self):
        log.info("daemon ready, keyboard=%s mouse=%s isos_dir=%s",
                  self.keyboard.path, self.mouse.path, self.storage.isos_dir)
        self._send_startup_state()

        while self.running:
            n = self.ser.in_waiting
            data = self.ser.read(n if n else 1)
            if not data:
                continue
            for frame_type, payload in self.parser.feed(data):
                self._handle_frame(frame_type, payload)

    def stop(self, *_args):
        self.running = False

    def shutdown(self):
        log.info("shutting down: releasing keys/buttons")
        try:
            self.keyboard.release_all()
            self.mouse.release_all_buttons()
        except Exception:
            pass
        self.keyboard.close()
        self.mouse.close()
        self.ser.close()

    def _send_startup_state(self):
        if self.storage.current_iso:
            self._send(protocol.encode_iso_mounted(self.storage.current_iso))
        else:
            self._send(protocol.encode_iso_ejected())

    def _send(self, frame_bytes):
        try:
            self.ser.write(frame_bytes)
        except serial.SerialException as e:
            log.warning("serial write failed: %s", e)

    def _handle_frame(self, frame_type, payload):
        p = protocol
        try:
            if frame_type == p.KEY_DOWN:
                self.keyboard.key_down(payload[0])
            elif frame_type == p.KEY_UP:
                self.keyboard.key_up(payload[0])
            elif frame_type == p.MOUSE_MOVE:
                dx, dy = p.decode_mouse_move(payload)
                self.mouse.move(dx, dy)
            elif frame_type == p.MOUSE_DOWN:
                self.mouse.button_down(payload[0])
            elif frame_type == p.MOUSE_UP:
                self.mouse.button_up(payload[0])
            elif frame_type == p.MOUSE_SCROLL:
                self.mouse.scroll(struct.unpack("b", payload)[0])
            elif frame_type == p.LIST_ISOS:
                names, current = self.storage.list_isos()
                self._send(p.encode_iso_list(names, current))
            elif frame_type == p.MOUNT_ISO:
                name = p.decode_mount_iso(payload)
                try:
                    self.storage.mount(name)
                    self._send(p.encode_iso_mounted(name))
                except ValueError as e:
                    self._send(p.encode_error(frame_type, str(e)))
            elif frame_type == p.EJECT_ISO:
                self.storage.eject()
                self._send(p.encode_iso_ejected())
            elif frame_type == p.AP_ENABLE:
                try:
                    self.wifi_ap.set_enabled(True)
                    self._send(p.encode_ap_status(self.wifi_ap.is_enabled()))
                except RuntimeError as e:
                    self._send(p.encode_error(frame_type, str(e)))
            elif frame_type == p.AP_DISABLE:
                try:
                    self.wifi_ap.set_enabled(False)
                    self._send(p.encode_ap_status(self.wifi_ap.is_enabled()))
                except RuntimeError as e:
                    self._send(p.encode_error(frame_type, str(e)))
            elif frame_type == p.AP_STATUS_QUERY:
                self._send(p.encode_ap_status(self.wifi_ap.is_enabled()))
            elif frame_type == p.PING:
                self._send(p.encode_pong())
            else:
                log.debug("unknown frame type 0x%02X", frame_type)
        except Exception as e:
            log.exception("error handling frame type 0x%02X", frame_type)
            self._send(p.encode_error(frame_type, str(e)))


def main():
    daemon = Daemon()
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, daemon.stop)
    signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, daemon.stop)
    try:
        daemon.run()
    finally:
        daemon.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```
4	Shared wire protocol for the laptop <-> Raspberry Pi KVM/crash-cart control
5	link (the USB-TTL serial link, separate from the Pi's USB OTG port which
6	carries HID/mass-storage to the target machine).
7	
8	This file must be identical on both ends -- copy it verbatim to the Pi
9	(see pi/install.sh) rather than maintaining two versions.
10	
11	Frame format:
12	    [0xAA sync][type: 1 byte][len: 2 bytes LE][payload: len bytes][checksum: 1 byte]
13	    checksum = (type byte + len bytes + payload bytes) summed, & 0xFF
14	
15	On a checksum mismatch the parser resyncs by discarding bytes until it
16	finds a sync byte that leads to a valid frame, rather than trusting a
17	possibly-corrupt length field.
18	"""
19	
20	import struct
21	
22	SYNC_BYTE = 0xAA
```

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 3:25:22 PM</sup>

Everything passes. Here's where things stand:

**Video graininess**: I couldn't fix this blind a second time, so instead of guessing again I added a startup print of the actually-negotiated capture mode (resolution/FOURCC/FPS). Run `client.py` and check that line — then open OBS's Video Capture Device properties dialog for the same card and compare its resolution/FPS/"Video Format" dropdown against what gets printed. If they don't match, pass the matching values via `--capture-fourcc`/`--capture-width`/`--capture-height` (that's the concrete lever now available). Tell me both sets of numbers if it's still off and I can pin it down precisely instead of guessing.

**Mouse — full redesign to touchscreen-style absolute positioning**, replacing relative capture entirely:
- **Wire protocol**: `MOUSE_MOVE` (relative dx/dy) → `MOUSE_ABSOLUTE` (x/y as a 0–32767 fraction of the target's whole screen — same convention QEMU's `usb-tablet` device uses).
- **Pi gadget** (`gadget-setup.sh`): the mouse HID function is now an absolute pointer (5 buttons + 16-bit X + 16-bit Y + relative wheel, 6-byte report) instead of a relative mouse. I wrote a small HID-descriptor walker to mechanically verify the hand-crafted bytes are well-formed (balanced collections, bit count sums to exactly 48 bits) rather than trusting it by eye, and confirmed the bytes actually in the file match byte-for-byte.
- **`pi/daemon.py`**: `HidMouse` now holds absolute x/y state (defaulting to center) instead of accumulating/splitting relative deltas — actually simpler than before.
- **`client.py`**: the whole capture-mode concept is gone — no more F9, no hidden/grabbed cursor, no "Mouse Capture: ON/OFF" indicator. Clicks are routed purely by Y position (menu bar strip vs. video area); a click/drag in the video area maps to a fraction of the displayed video content (clamped into it, so letterbox bars don't dead-zone) and moves+clicks the target there. A button released after dragging out of the video area still gets forwarded, so it can't get stuck down on the target.

**Important**: this needs `sudo ./install.sh` re-run + a reboot on the Pi to take effect — an already-bound gadget won't pick up the new HID report shape on its own. Noted in the README's troubleshooting section.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 5:13:12 PM</sup>

Found it. That's a very specific symptom — bottom-right corner is exactly where Windows' "Show Desktop" sliver lives — and it points straight at my own DPI-awareness fix from last time. Calling Windows' `SetProcessDpiAwareness()` directly via `ctypes` bypasses SDL's own DPI bookkeeping, so SDL's mouse-event coordinates ended up scaled relative to the window's actual pixel buffer size. Since `map_click_to_target` clamps into `video_rect`, every click coordinate that came out too large clamped straight to the bottom-right corner. Let me fix this properly — SDL has its own documented mechanism for this that keeps its internal coordinate space consistent.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 5:16:08 PM</sup>

Both fixed:

**Video**: `--capture-width`/`--capture-height` now default to `1920`/`1080` (matching what worked for you), instead of leaving the capture card to silently negotiate whatever it wants. Pass `0` for either to opt back out if your setup needs a different native resolution.

**Mouse**: your diagnosis ("always registers at the bottom-right corner") pinpointed it exactly — that's Windows' "Show Desktop" sliver, explaining the minimize/restore-all toggle. Root cause: my earlier DPI-awareness fix called Windows' `SetProcessDpiAwareness()` directly via `ctypes`, which desynced SDL's internal notion of the window's coordinate space from Windows' actual scaled coordinates. Every mouse event's position came out scaled up relative to the window's real pixel size, and since `map_click_to_target()` clamps out-of-range coordinates into the video rect, every click clamped to the corner. Fixed by switching to the `SDL_WINDOWS_DPI_AWARENESS` environment variable (set before `pygame.init()`), which is SDL's own supported mechanism and keeps its coordinate bookkeeping self-consistent instead of being blindsided by an external API call.

Full test suite still passes. Given this class of bug (coordinate-space mismatch) isn't really something my existing tests can catch without a real Windows display + real DPI scaling — it only showed up on actual hardware — it'd be worth confirming on your end that clicks now land where you actually click before calling it done.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 5:44:54 PM</sup>

Fixed. Quick check first — your message started with a lone "mouse" before the serial report cut off; is that confirming the click-position fix from last time is working now, or is there still something off with the mouse?

On the serial issue, this was a real, findable bug (not hardware-dependent guessing this time):

- **Root cause**: Windows' USB selective suspend puts an idle USB-serial adapter to sleep, and the first read/write after waking throws exactly that `WriteFile`/`ERROR_BAD_COMMAND` error. A target reboot naturally creates an idle gap (waiting for POST) right before you start mashing F1 — that's the trigger.
- **Compounding bug**: `client.py`'s background reader thread died permanently on the *first* serial error it ever hit (a bare `return` in the except clause), and writes just logged the error and gave up — so once the port hiccuped once, every future key/mouse send silently failed and every Pi reply was dropped forever, matching "have to restart the client to fix it."

Fixed both: read and write paths now close and reopen the port and retry once instead of giving up, and the client sends a lightweight keepalive (reusing the existing `PING`/`PONG` frames) whenever the link's been idle 2+ seconds, so Windows shouldn't consider the port idle enough to suspend in the first place. Verified this against a fake serial port that simulates the exact failure (write throws once, then a fresh handle must pick up the retry; a read failure must not kill the reader thread) — full output:

```
write-path reopen-and-retry OK
keepalive-when-idle OK
read-path survives failure without killing the reader thread OK
```

Also documented the belt-and-suspenders fix in the README: disabling "Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power" for the adapter (and its USB hub) in Device Manager, in case suspension still sneaks in somehow.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 6:53:08 PM</sup>

Found it, and it's my own design flaw — I explicitly noted the AP toggle blocks the whole daemon loop "for a few seconds" as an accepted tradeoff, but that assumption is wrong: `subprocess.run(timeout=)` only kills the *direct* child. If `wifi-ap-toggle.sh` (or anything it calls — `nmcli`, `hostapd`, etc.) leaves behind a process still holding the captured stdout/stderr pipes open, the read blocks forever regardless of the nominal timeout, freezing the entire single-threaded daemon — including keyboard/mouse — until you restart it. That explains "any button" too: once the daemon's truly wedged, everything looks broken from then on, not just the thing that actually triggered it.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 6:59:58 PM</sup>

Found and fixed a real, serious one in `pi/daemon.py`. The daemon is single-threaded by design, and the AP commands (Network menu) used to run inline — but `subprocess.run(timeout=...)` only kills the *direct* child on timeout, not any grandchild it spawned (`nmcli`, `hostapd`, etc.). If one of those got left holding the captured stdout/stderr pipes open, the read blocked forever regardless of the nominal timeout — freezing the daemon's entire read-parse-handle loop, keyboard and mouse included, until you restarted it. That also explains "any button" triggering it: once the daemon's actually wedged, *everything* looks broken from then on — the real trigger is specifically an AP status check or enable/disable, not the other menus.

Fixed two ways:
- AP commands now run on a background thread, so they can never block keyboard/mouse regardless of how long they take or whether they hang outright.
- `WifiApController.set_enabled()` now runs `wifi-ap-toggle.sh` in its own process group and kills the *whole group* on timeout (not just the immediate script process), so a hang actually gets cleaned up rather than merely contained.

Verified mechanically: a test simulates an action that hangs indefinitely and confirms the daemon's main-loop-facing call returns immediately regardless, plus the Popen-based timeout/success/failure paths (including the process-group-kill path) all pass. Full suite still green.

This needs `sudo ./install.sh` re-run + reboot on the Pi to pick up (same as the earlier mouse-descriptor change — daemon.py is just copied into `/opt/kvmdongle/`, so the fix takes effect as soon as the service restarts with the new file in place; a reboot isn't strictly required this time, just restarting `kvmdongle-daemon`, but re-running `install.sh` is the easiest way to get the updated file onto the Pi).

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 7:54:26 PM</sup>

Two distinct, serious bugs here. Let me take them one at a time.

**The segfault** is a genuine thread-safety bug I introduced: my `_reopen()` only locked its own close+recreate sequence, not the actual read/write calls — so the reader thread could be mid-`read()` on the old handle at the exact moment the write path (main thread) closed it out from under it. On Windows, pyserial's overlapped-I/O structures get torn down by `close()`, and closing one while another thread has an in-flight operation on it is undefined behavior — that's exactly the `_overlapped_read` becoming `None` mid-read, and the segfault.

**The BIOS mouse freeze** is a different, plausible bug: the daemon writes HID reports to `/dev/hidg1` *inline*, blocking. If the BIOS's USB stack enumerates the mouse but doesn't promptly poll/consume its interrupt endpoint (much more likely in a minimal BIOS environment than in Windows), that `write()` call can block indefinitely — freezing the single-threaded daemon's entire loop, keyboard included, until you restart it. That matches "works fine in Windows" perfectly.

Let me fix both.

## Assistant <sup>7/30/2026, 8:11:22 PM</sup>

Both fixed. Summary:

**The segfault** — a genuine thread-safety bug in my earlier reconnect fix: the lock only covered `_reopen()`'s own close-and-recreate sequence, not the actual read/write calls. The reader thread could be mid-`read()` on the port at the exact moment the write path closed it out from under it during a reopen. On Windows, pyserial's overlapped-I/O structures get torn down by `close()`, and touching them from a read still in flight on another thread corrupted memory badly enough to crash the process rather than raise a catchable exception. Fixed with a single reentrant lock guarding *every* touch of the serial handle, redesigned so the read loop never blocks while holding it (only reads bytes already confirmed waiting; sleeps outside the lock otherwise) — so a reopen is never stuck waiting behind a long read, and a read can never happen concurrently with a close.

Verified this one carefully, since a lock bug that only shows up under real contention is exactly the kind of thing that's easy to "fix" without actually fixing: wrote a stress test with a fake serial port whose `read()` deliberately takes a moment (simulating an in-flight overlapped read) and asserts `close()` is never called while a read is in progress, under concurrent write/reopen pressure. Then, as a negative control, reconstructed the *old* buggy locking pattern against the same harness — it flagged 26 violations, confirming the test would have caught the real bug, not just decoration.

**The BIOS mouse freeze** — `/dev/hidg*` writes were blocking file descriptors. A `write()` to a USB HID gadget device can block if the host isn't promptly polling that endpoint, and a BIOS/UEFI's minimal USB stack is far more likely to do that than a full OS (matches "works fine in Windows" exactly). Since the daemon is single-threaded, one stalled mouse write froze the whole loop, keyboard included. Fixed by opening those file descriptors `O_NONBLOCK` — the existing error handling already just logs and drops a report it can't send, no other code needed to change.

Full test suite (protocol, daemon, client, menubar, AP, video, letterbox, click-mapping, reconnect, race) passes. Both fixes need `sudo ./install.sh` re-run (daemon.py gets copied fresh) — no reboot required this time, just restarting `kvmdongle-daemon`.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 12:56:32 AM</sup>

Both fixed and tested. Full details in the README, but briefly:

- **Dropdown clicks leaking to the target**: a real regression from the touchscreen redesign — I routed clicks purely by `y < MENU_HEIGHT`, but an open dropdown's items are drawn *below* that strip, so clicking one fell into "video area" territory and got forwarded instead of activating the item. Fixed by trying the menu bar first (it knows its own real extent) and only forwarding if it says the click wasn't its.
- **Plain click moves cursor but doesn't click**: direct side effect of last session's `O_NONBLOCK` fix for the BIOS freeze. A plain click sends position-then-button-down with zero gap; if the gadget's small endpoint queue hadn't finished draining the first report, the second (non-blocking) write could hit a transient `EAGAIN` and get silently dropped. Drag was fine because its motion reports have natural gaps. Fixed with a bounded retry (~10ms worst case) — long enough to cover normal drain time, short enough that a genuinely non-polling host (BIOS) still can't freeze the daemon.

On the reboot/BIOS-input issue — I've now addressed everything on the software side I can think of (reconnect+keepalive on the client, non-blocking+retrying HID writes and backgrounded AP commands on the daemon). If it's still not getting through, I suspect it's actually hardware:

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 12:58:47 AM</sup>

Very useful — that fully rules out a Pi power-loss/reboot as the cause. Given that, plus everything else I've now fixed on both the client and daemon sides (reconnect, keepalive, non-blocking retrying HID writes, backgrounded AP commands), I think what's left is likely a hardware/firmware timing issue rather than a remaining software bug:

When the target reboots, its own USB host controller goes through a full re-enumeration of every USB device as part of POST — including our composite gadget (keyboard + mouse + mass storage, which is more complex to enumerate than a plain keyboard). That takes real time, and many BIOSes only listen for the "enter setup" keypress in a fairly short window right after POST starts. If our gadget's re-enumeration hasn't finished by the time that window closes, F1 presses sent during it simply never reach a USB host controller that isn't listening yet — nothing our daemon or client can do about that, since it's the target's firmware, not our link, that isn't ready.

Two things worth trying to confirm/work around this:

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 1:44:03 AM</sup>

Fixed properly this time. Summary:

The retry-with-backoff from last round was treating a symptom, not the cause. The real issue: position and buttons were being sent as two independently-timed frames/writes (move, then a separate button-down), but a real HID absolute pointer always reports a complete position+button snapshot in one sample — never split. "Unreliable specifically at the same position" was the key clue: a click without movement sends a position report identical to the one already in effect, immediately followed by a button-only report, and that pairing was fragile in a way a genuinely new position wasn't.

Fixed by redesigning the protocol so position and buttons travel together atomically:
- **`protocol.py`**: `MOUSE_ABSOLUTE` + `MOUSE_DOWN`/`MOUSE_UP` → one `MOUSE_STATE` frame carrying x, y, *and* the button bitmask together.
- **`pi/daemon.py`**: `HidMouse.move_to()`/`button_down()`/`button_up()` → one `set_state(x, y, buttons)` that does a single atomic write.
- **`client.py`**: every mouse event (down, up, drag) now computes and sends the complete desired state in one call, instead of a position write followed by a separate button write.

The retry logic from last round stays in place as defense-in-depth (still useful if the endpoint is genuinely busy), but it's no longer doing the heavy lifting. Updated all the affected tests (protocol round-trip, daemon report assembly — including a test that a single `set_state()` call produces exactly one write) and everything passes.

This is a protocol change between `client.py` and `pi/daemon.py`, so it needs `sudo ./install.sh` + restarting `kvmdongle-daemon` on the Pi to take effect.

```
1	"""
```

```
3	
4	Shared wire protocol for the laptop <-> Raspberry Pi KVM/crash-cart control
5	link (the USB-TTL serial link, separate from the Pi's USB OTG port which

8	This file must be identical on both ends -- copy it verbatim to the Pi
9	(see pi/install.sh) rather than maintaining two versions.
10	
11	Frame format:
12	    [0xAA sync][type: 1 byte][len: 2 bytes LE][payload: len bytes][checksum: 1 byte]
13	    checksum = (type byte + len bytes + payload bytes) summed, & 0xFF
14	
15	On a checksum mismatch the parser resyncs by discarding bytes until it
16	finds a sync byte that leads to a valid frame, rather than trusting a
17	possibly-corrupt length field.
18	"""
19	
20	import struct
21	
22	SYNC_BYTE = 0xAA
23	
24	# Laptop -> Pi
25	KEY_DOWN = 0x01
26	KEY_UP = 0x02
27	MOUSE_STATE = 0x03
28	MOUSE_SCROLL = 0x06
29	LIST_ISOS = 0x10
30	MOUNT_ISO = 0x11
31	EJECT_ISO = 0x12
32	PING = 0x13
33	AP_ENABLE = 0x14
```

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 3:04:05 AM</sup>

Went through every file. Summary of what I found and cleaned up:

- **`protocol.py`**: removed `ACK`/`encode_ack` — dead code left over from early design, never actually used since every command ended up with its own specific typed reply (`ISO_MOUNTED`, `AP_STATUS`, `PONG`, etc.) instead of a generic acknowledgment.
- **`pi/daemon.py`**: fixed a docstring that still said replies came back as "ACK/ERROR/ISO_LIST/etc." — corrected to name the actual reply types.
- **`client.py`**: removed a small unnecessary indirection — `MOUSE_LEFT`/`MOUSE_RIGHT`/`MOUSE_MIDDLE` were aliased from `protocol.*` at module level just to save a few characters at two call sites; now those two sites reference `protocol.MOUSE_LEFT` etc. directly.

Everything else — `daemon.py`'s HID/storage/AP classes, all the shell scripts, systemd units, config files, `webui.py`, `requirements.txt` — was already clean; no other dead code, unused imports, or orphaned functions turned up. I grepped the whole repo for every symbol renamed or removed over the course of this session (`MOUSE_ABSOLUTE`, `MOUSE_DOWN`/`UP`, `move_to`/`button_down`/`button_up`, `mouse_capture`, `set_mouse_capture`, etc.) to make sure nothing stale was left behind in code or comments, and reran the full test suite after each change — still all green.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 12:45:35 PM</sup>

Yes, close — one clarification on direction. That's `[from pi] type=0x85 payload=b''` you're seeing (PONG, type `0x85`), and it's the *reply* half of the keepalive, not the Pi initiating anything on its own.

Here's the actual flow:
- `client.py` (laptop side) tracks how long it's been since it last sent anything, and if the link's been idle 2+ seconds, sends a `PING` — see `send_keepalive_if_idle()` at [client.py:307-308](client.py#L307-L308).
- `pi/daemon.py` just echoes a `PONG` back for any `PING` it receives.
- Since `PONG` isn't one of the "handled quietly" types, the debug branch at [client.py:868](client.py#L868) prints it as `[from pi] type=0x85 payload=b''`.

So it's the laptop keeping the USB-serial link active (to stop Windows from putting the adapter to sleep via USB selective suspend during idle stretches — e.g. while a target is rebooting), and the Pi dutifully answering. Nothing to worry about if you see it periodically during quiet stretches.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 1:00:02 PM</sup>

Done. Added a small status light to the top-right of the menu bar:

- **`SerialLink`**: now tracks the timestamp of the last frame received from the Pi (any frame — a `PONG`, an ISO list reply, whatever), and exposes `is_connected()`, true if something arrived within the last 5 seconds. Since the client already sends a keepalive `PING` whenever the link's been idle 2+ seconds, there's always something recent to judge this by even during quiet stretches.
- **`MenuBar`**: draws a small filled circle in the top-right corner — green when connected, red when not (including honestly starting red at launch, before any reply has ever arrived, rather than assuming the best).

Tested both pieces directly: the timing logic (disconnected before any reply, connected right after one, disconnected again once it's aged past the timeout) and the color decision (connected → green, disconnected → red, and no-callback-supplied doesn't error). Full suite still passes.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 1:42:34 PM</sup>

Done. Added a **Video** menu next to Storage/Network:

- Lists detected capture device indices, marks the active one with `*`, and has a **Refresh** item to re-scan.
- Clicking a different device closes the old `VideoStream` and opens the new one — the window doesn't resize or restart, since the existing letterbox/aspect-fit rendering already recomputes scale per-frame regardless of source resolution.
- If opening the new device fails, the old one is left running untouched (only swapped over after the new one confirms `isOpened()`), so a bad selection can't leave you with no video at all.
- The currently-active device is never reopened just to confirm it's still there during a scan — some backends won't allow a second concurrent open, and even where they would, there's no reason to risk disrupting a working stream just to double-check it.

Also factored the "negotiated capture mode" description (used at startup for the OBS-comparison troubleshooting) into a small `describe_negotiated_mode()` helper, reused when switching devices too, so you get the same resolution/format confirmation printed to the terminal after a switch.

Tested the scanning/skip logic and the formatter directly against a fake `cv2.VideoCapture` (confirms the active index is reported without being reopened, others are probed and filtered correctly) — full suite still green.

```
1	# KVM / Crash-Cart Dongle
2	
3	A DIY KVM/crash-cart: an HDMI-capture+VGA dongle handles video (separate,
4	out of scope here), while a Raspberry Pi Zero W plugged into the target
5	machine's USB port emulates a keyboard, mouse, and a read-only CD-ROM
6	(backed by an ISO already on the Pi's SD card) -- enough to remote-control
7	a machine and install an OS on it. Your laptop talks to the Pi over a
8	USB-TTL serial adapter wired to the Pi's GPIO UART, running the app in
9	[client.py](client.py).
10	
11	`old/` contains a previous, Arduino-based generation of this project, kept
12	for reference -- its UI is what `client.py` is modeled on.
13	
14	## Hardware
15	
16	- Raspberry Pi Zero W
17	- A blank/fresh [DietPi](https://dietpi.com/) SD card -- used instead of
```

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 3:38:15 PM</sup>

Both features are done. Summary of what was added in this session:

**Serial Port menu** — mirrors the existing Video menu: lists detected ports (active one marked `*`), with a Refresh item. Switching only swaps `link` over after the new port opens successfully, so a bad port name never disrupts the working connection. Also fixed a latent stale-bound-method bug on `link.is_connected` (and proactively on `terminal.link`) that would've kept pointing at a dead link object after a port switch.

**Pi shell / terminal overlay** — new "Terminal" menu item ("Open Pi Shell", F12 to close). It spawns a real `bash` via `pty.fork()` on the Pi (`ShellSession` in [pi/daemon.py](pi/daemon.py)), tunnels raw bytes both ways over four new frame types in [protocol.py](protocol.py) (`SHELL_OPEN/CLOSE/INPUT/RESIZE` → `SHELL_OUTPUT/CLOSED`), and renders it client-side with `pyte` as a full ANSI/VT100 terminal (`TerminalOverlay` in [client.py](client.py)) — colors, cursor, interactive programs all work, so it behaves like an SSH session even though it's carried over the same serial link used for KB/mouse/storage. While open, all keyboard/mouse input is captured by the shell instead of the target.

Testing: full suite (protocol, daemon, shell session with faked PTY/fcntl/termios, client menu/terminal logic, plus every pre-existing test) passes. `pyte` added to `requirements.txt`, and [README.md](README.md) now documents both features under Controls plus two Troubleshooting entries (missing `pyte`, and the need to `sudo ./install.sh` + restart the daemon on the Pi since this adds new wire-protocol frame types).

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 3:56:52 PM</sup>

The Pi shell now opens as a genuine separate OS window instead of an overlay:

**Architecture**: pygame/SDL only supports one window per process, so the terminal is now a second process — [terminal_window.py](terminal_window.py) — spawned by [client.py](client.py)'s new `TerminalWindow` class. That controller does no rendering at all; it's a pure byte relay between the real serial link and the child's stdin/stdout, reusing the exact same wire framing (`protocol.encode`/`FrameParser`, the `SHELL_*` frame types) as the real laptop↔Pi link, just over a local pipe instead of serial.

**What changed in client.py**: `TerminalOverlay` (which drew on top of the video and stole all keyboard/mouse input while open) is gone, replaced by the much smaller `TerminalWindow` relay. The main window's event loop lost all its terminal-awareness — no more F12 interception, no more "don't forward mouse/keyboard while terminal is open" guards — since the two windows are now genuinely independent and the OS handles focus routing naturally. F12 now just forwards to the target like any other function key again.

**New file, terminal_window.py**: opens its own resizable pygame window titled "Pi Shell," renders the pyte screen buffer with real ANSI colors/cursor, translates local keystrokes to VT100 byte sequences, and shows a "[session closed]" banner (rather than vanishing) if the Pi's bash exits on its own — closing on F12 or the window's own close button either way.

Tested: the relay logic (open/close/notify_closed/feed, bidirectional frame forwarding, orphan-prevention on unexpected child exit) with a fake subprocess wired to real OS pipes, the pure helper functions (`fit`, `translate_key`, `draw`) against real `pyte`, and — since a real display is available on this machine — an actual end-to-end smoke test that spawned the real child process, exchanged real frames, and confirmed it renders and shuts down cleanly. Full existing regression suite still green. README's Controls/Troubleshooting sections updated to describe the separate-window behavior.

The only reply this can ever\n        send is an ERROR, and only for the synchronous, fast failure of\n        not being able to launch the command at all (e.g. systemctl\n        missing) -- a real restart/reboot/shutdown gives no success reply,\n        since whatever would send one is exactly what's going away.\"\"\"\n        try:\n            subprocess.Popen(argv)\n        except OSError as e:\n            self._send(protocol.encode_error(frame_type, str(e)))\n\n    def _run_ap_async(self, frame_type, action):"
```json
}
```

```json
  "new_string": "class ArmedAction:\n    \"\"\"A confirm-to-execute guard for menu items with real physical\n    consequences (Reboot/Shutdown Pi) that the rest of this app's\n    one-click menu items (Eject, Mount, AP toggle) don't have -- a\n    Pi Zero W has no remote power button, so an accidental Shutdown click\n    means someone has to walk over and physically power-cycle it.\n\n    The first click arms it (the menu item's own label changes to prompt\n    a second click); a second click within ARM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS actually\n    fires. Nothing tracks menu open/close explicitly -- the short timeout\n    alone is the disarm mechanism, since MenuBar already closes a dropdown\n    after every item click, so reopening the same menu to click again is\n    the normal path to confirming, not something to treat as cancelling.\"\"\"\n\n    ARM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 4.0\n\n    def __init__(self):\n        self._armed_at = None\n\n    def is_armed(self):\n        return self._armed_at is not None and (time.monotonic() - self._armed_at) < self.ARM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS\n\n    def arm(self):\n        self._armed_at = time.monotonic()\n\n    def disarm(self):\n        self._armed_at = None\n\n\nclass MenuBar:"
}
```

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 4:16:21 PM</sup>

All done. Summary of what was added:

**Protocol** ([protocol.py](protocol.py)): three new no-payload frame types — `RESTART_DAEMON`, `REBOOT_PI`, `SHUTDOWN_PI` — with encoders. None get a success reply, since whatever would send one (the daemon process, or the whole Pi) is exactly what's going away.

**Daemon** ([pi/daemon.py](pi/daemon.py)): a `_trigger_system_action()` helper fires the matching `systemctl restart kvmdongle-daemon` / `systemctl reboot` / `systemctl poweroff` via a fire-and-forget `Popen` (not `run()`, so it never blocks the main loop waiting on a command that may outlive this process). The only reply it can ever send is an `ERROR`, for the synchronous case where the command can't even launch.

**Client** ([client.py](client.py)): `SerialLink` gained matching `send_restart_daemon`/`send_reboot_pi`/`send_shutdown_pi`. Per your answer, Restart Daemon is a plain one-click item, while Reboot Pi and Shutdown Pi use a new `ArmedAction` guard — first click arms it (label changes to "...click again to confirm"), a second click within 4 seconds actually sends it, arming one disarms the other, and it silently disarms itself if you don't confirm in time.

Tested: protocol round-trip, daemon frame dispatch (correct `systemctl` argv per command, `ERROR` reply only on launch failure) via a stripped `DummyDaemon`, `ArmedAction`'s arm/disarm/timeout behavior and the reboot/shutdown wiring, and `SerialLink`'s new send methods — all green alongside the full existing suite. README's Controls and Troubleshooting sections updated, including the note that this is another protocol change requiring `sudo ./install.sh` + daemon restart on the Pi.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 5:24:38 PM</sup>

This is happening below your code — it's a raw USB enumeration failure between the target's `xhci_hcd` (host controller) and the Pi's `dwc2` (peripheral controller), not something `daemon.py`/`protocol.py` can see or retry. A few things worth knowing:

**What the errors mean**: `-110` is `-ETIMEDOUT`. "device descriptor read/64, error -110" means the target's controller did a bus reset and then timed out reading the first 64 bytes of the gadget's descriptor during re-enumeration — pure USB-PHY/timing failure, before any HID/mass-storage driver even gets involved. `usbhid ... can't add hid device -110` is the HID driver's bind attempt failing for the same reason on that pass — which is exactly why it doesn't reliably correlate with actually-broken input: the composite gadget usually finishes re-enumerating correctly a moment later, and that one HID bind attempt was just caught mid-reset.

**Why Windows doesn't show it**: this is a well-known behavioral gap, not something specific to this gadget's descriptors — Windows' USB stack (`usbccgp.sys`/`usbhub.sys`) tolerates marginal enumeration timing and weaker signal integrity far better than Linux's `xhci_hcd`, which resets and logs much more aggressively on the same borderline signal. Pi Zero (W) gadget mode + Linux hosts hitting exactly this message pair is a widely reported combination.

Given it reproduces on two very different Linux boxes (ThinkCentre, R530) but not a Windows laptop, the common factor is Linux's stricter enumeration timing, and the likely trigger is a marginal high-speed (480Mbps) link. In order of cheapest-to-try:

1. **Cable** — the single most common real fix for this exact message. A worn/cheap/long micro-USB cable is the classic cause of high-speed signal-integrity failures that Linux flags and Windows shrugs off. Try a short, known-good data-rated cable first.
2. **Pi's power supply on PWR IN** — a marginal 5V supply can brown out the Zero W's CPU just long enough to miss the tight interrupt deadline `dwc2` needs to service `ep0`, which the host then sees as this same timeout.
3. **Force full-speed (12Mbps) as a diagnostic**: add `dwc2.speed=1` (cmdline.txt module param). If that makes it disappear, it confirms a high-speed signal-margin issue — you can then decide whether to keep it (costs ISO-mount throughput, doesn't matter for HID) or go chase the cable/supply now that it's confirmed.
4. Does it correlate with anything — ISO mount/eject, AP toggling — or does it happen at idle too? That would point at CPU-latency-under-load vs. pure physical-layer flakiness.

Want me to add the `dwc2.speed=1` option (documented, opt-in) to `install.sh`/README so you can test #3 easily, or do you want to try the cable/supply first and report back?

Given the cable swap didn't help, I want to redirect the hypothesis rather than push further into device-tree overlay territory. Cable/signal-integrity theory is looking weaker now — let's check something that fits the evidence better: **USB autosuspend on the target**.

The exact log line you got — `reset high-speed USB device number 34 using xhci_hcd` — is also the classic signature of a Linux host autosuspending an idle USB device and then failing to cleanly resume it, falling back to a full bus reset/re-enumeration instead. This fits your evidence well:
- Cable swap not helping argues against pure signal-integrity/cabling as the cause.
- It's Linux-specific in your testing — autosuspend defaults/behavior differ meaningfully between Linux's `usbcore` and Windows' USB stack.
- The gadget currently declares itself as **not supporting remote wakeup** (`bmAttributes = 0x80` in `gadget-setup.sh` — only the "bus-powered" bit is set), so if the host suspends it, there's no clean way for it to signal "wake me up," which is exactly the kind of situation that forces a hard reset on resume instead of a graceful wake.

**Quick, no-reboot test** — first find the device:
```
lsusb
```
Look for `ID 1d6b:0104 Linux Foundation Multifunction Composite Gadget`, note its Bus/Device numbers (or just use the `3-9` you already have from the `usbhid 3-9:1.1` line — that's the sysfs bus-port ID).

Check its current power setting:
```
cat /sys/bus/usb/devices/3-9/power/control
```
It'll say `auto` (autosuspend allowed) or `on` (always on). Force it on live, no reboot:
```
echo on | sudo tee /sys/bus/usb/devices/3-9/power/control
```
Then use the KVM normally — including leaving it idle for a stretch and coming back to it, since that's the trigger pattern for autosuspend specifically — and watch `sudo journalctl -k -f` for the reset messages.

One thing that'll help me weight this: **does the reset tend to happen after a period of no keyboard/mouse activity**, or does it also happen during continuous use? That distinction is the strongest signal for whether autosuspend is really the culprit here.

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 11:30:12 PM</sup>

This dmesg is very informative and points somewhere different than cable/signal-integrity. Walking through the timeline:

```
23:24:53  fully enumerates — keyboard interface (1.0) binds and works
23:25:14  mouse interface (1.1) fails to bind: -110        <- odd, but separate issue
23:25:24  storage interface (1.2) binds fine
  ...33 seconds of nothing...
23:25:57  device gets RESET (unprompted) — starts the death spiral
```

The keyboard interface enumerated cleanly and worked for a full ~60+ seconds. That's a very different failure mode than a marginal/flaky cable (which would show corruption-type errors continuously or fail immediately, not run clean for a minute then suddenly die). And you confirmed the break happened right when you went back to actually use the keyboard after it had been sitting idle — that's the classic signature of **USB autosuspend + a failed resume**.

Here's why that fits: your gadget's descriptor (`gadget-setup.sh`, `bmAttributes = 0x80`) explicitly declares **no remote-wakeup support**. If Linux autosuspends an idle device that can't do remote wakeup, the *only* way to bring it back is a full bus reset instead of a graceful resume — exactly the `reset high-speed USB device` line, and if that particular reset-based resume fails on this `dwc2` implementation, you get stuck retrying forever, which matches your loop exactly. This also explains the Windows-vs-Linux difference better than the cable/speed theories did: Linux's default USB autosuspend behavior is considerably more aggressive than Windows' for devices that don't explicitly opt out.

**To confirm**, right after a fresh connect (before any reset has happened), check:
```
cat /sys/bus/usb/devices/1-1/power/control
```
If it says `auto`, that's autosuspend enabled for this device. Force it off live:
```
echo on | sudo tee /sys/bus/usb/devices/1-1/power/control
```
then deliberately leave the keyboard/mouse untouched for a couple minutes and see if it survives past the point where it previously died.

If that confirms it, there's a clean permanent fix that needs zero configuration on whatever target you plug into (important, since you can't install udev rules on every random machine you crash-cart into): have `daemon.py` periodically re-send the current HID state as a no-op "keepalive" report (say, every ~1 second) whenever nothing else has gone out recently — same pattern this project already uses for the laptop↔Pi serial link's own idle/suspend problem (`SerialLink.send_keepalive_if_idle()`). Constant, harmless bus traffic means the host's idle timer never reaches the autosuspend threshold in the first place, regardless of what any given target's default policy is.

Want to test the `power/control` theory first, or should I go ahead and add the keepalive to `daemon.py` now on the assumption this is it?

## Assistant <sup>7/31/2026, 11:40:30 PM</sup>

Good — that rules out autosuspend cleanly (`on`, not `auto`, means it was never in play). Let me look at the timeline again with that eliminated, because there's a much better fit I skipped past.

```
23:25:24  usb-storage 1-1:1.2: USB Mass Storage device detected   <- storage interface binds, SCSI scan begins
   ...33 seconds...
23:25:57  usb 1-1: reset high-speed USB device number 23          <- unprompted reset
```

**33 seconds is suspiciously close to the Linux SCSI/usb-storage layer's default command timeout** (~30s). Here's the mechanism: when `usb-storage` binds a LUN, it runs SCSI INQUIRY / TEST UNIT READY / READ CAPACITY against it as part of setup. Your mass-storage LUN has **no ISO mounted** at boot by design (`lun.0/file` starts empty — that's intentional, per `gadget-setup.sh`). If the gadget's response to one of those commands against an empty/no-medium CD-ROM LUN stalls or doesn't come back cleanly, the SCSI layer's command timeout fires, and `usb-storage`'s error-recovery path for a timed-out command is a **full USB device reset** — which is exactly the line you're seeing, and it would also explain why it loops (the same problem recurs on every reset attempt).

This fits your evidence much better than anything before it:
- Explains why keyboard worked fine for a solid minute — the reset isn't a HID/keyboard problem at all, it's collateral damage from storage's reset, which takes keyboard/mouse down with it since the *whole device* gets reset.
- Explains your very first observation, that the mouse's `can't add hid device -110` "usually doesn't correspond with non-working input" — because that was never the real problem; it's a separate, mostly-harmless hiccup, and the actual persistent breakage comes from storage.
- Plausibly explains the Windows-vs-Linux gap too — Windows' mass-storage class driver may simply be more tolerant of an empty/no-medium LUN's responses than Linux's `usb-storage` reset-on-timeout behavior.

**Two quick tests, in order of how cleanly they isolate this:**

1. Comment out just the mass-storage symlink in `gadget-setup.sh` (keep both HID functions) and re-run/reboot:
```bash
ln -s functions/hid.usb0          configs/c.1/
ln -s functions/hid.usb1          configs/c.1/
# ln -s functions/mass_storage.usb0 configs/c.1/
```
If keyboard/mouse now stay rock-solid indefinitely with storage absent entirely, that confirms it's the mass-storage function causing the reset.

2. Alternative, keeping storage enabled: mount an actual ISO right after boot (so the LUN has real media instead of being empty) before the ~30s window elapses, and see if *that* avoids the reset — this would pin it down specifically to the empty-LUN case rather than mass storage in general.

Want to try #1 first? It's the faster, more decisive test.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 12:20:30 AM</sup>

That's a solid, clean confirmation — mass storage was the trigger for the reset loop, and two separate xHCI hosts both went stable the moment it was removed. Good diagnosis.

On the leftover `usbhid 1-1:1.1: can't add hid device: -110` for the mouse interface: it appeared once and never got a follow-up success line (compare to the keyboard, which logged both an `input:` line *and* a `hid-generic ... input,hidraw0` bind line — the mouse only got neither). That makes me want to double check: **did you actually confirm mouse movement/clicks worked during that 20-minute test**, or was it mainly keyboard you were exercising? If the mouse interface genuinely never bound, it might *look* fine because nothing forced you to notice, not because it's actually functional.

Bigger picture, there's a real decision to make now: mass storage (ISO mounting) is a documented core feature of this project, not something to just quietly drop. A few ways forward:

1. **Keep storage disabled** — simplest, ships a fully stable HID-only KVM today, loses ISO-mount entirely.
2. **Investigate the empty-LUN theory further** — my hypothesis was that an empty/no-medium CD-ROM LUN is what the storage class driver's probe chokes on. If that's right, always keeping *some* valid backing file in the LUN (a tiny placeholder ISO) instead of leaving it truly empty at boot might dodge the failure while keeping the feature. Worth testing before assuming it's unfixable.
3. **Re-enable storage but make it opt-in at runtime** — bind the mass-storage function only when the user actually wants to mount something, accepting that doing so mid-session would briefly disrupt keyboard/mouse (a real tradeoff, since that's exactly what the current design deliberately avoids).

Given ISO mounting is a whole feature people rely on, I'd lean toward trying #2 next since it's cheap to test and might get you both reliability and the feature — but it's your call. Want to check the mouse first, then decide?

Good catch to ask — since the LUN is configured with `cdrom=1`, a working mass-storage bind would show up as `/dev/sr0` (a SCSI CD-ROM device), **not** `/dev/sdX` (that naming is for plain disk-type LUNs). Look for lines like `sr0: scsi3-mmc drive` or `cdrom: Uniform CD-ROM driver` in dmesg — if none of those ever appear, the SCSI identification phase still isn't completing even with a real file behind the LUN.

That it still reset even with `netboot.xyz.iso` loaded is an important result, though — it means my "empty LUN specifically" theory was wrong (or at least incomplete). Since removing mass storage entirely *did* fix it, but populating the LUN did *not*, the trigger isn't "empty vs. populated" — it's something about the mass-storage function itself being present and active, possibly something that only kicks in once the host starts actually reading real blocks from it (e.g. `udev`/`blkid` probing the filesystem the moment `/dev/sr0` appears), rather than the earlier lightweight INQUIRY/TEST-UNIT-READY exchange.

Confirmed and important: **no `/dev/sr0` ever appeared, even with a real ISO loaded** — the SCSI probe still stalls at exactly the same point (right after `scsi host5: usb-storage 1-1:1.2`, ~32s before the reset). That rules out my "empty LUN" theory entirely — it's not about what's behind the LUN, it's something about the mass-storage *function* itself failing to properly service SCSI commands over its bulk endpoints, full stop.

Also worth flagging: the tail of this log is worse than earlier captures — it doesn't just loop the same reset, it degrades into `xhci_hcd: Timeout while waiting for setup device command`, `device not accepting address`, a port power-cycle attempt, and finally `unable to enumerate USB device`. That's the gadget's control endpoint getting progressively more wedged with each failed reset, not just repeating the same soft failure.

New leading theory: this looks like a **FIFO/endpoint-bandwidth contention issue specific to BCM2835's `dwc2`** — it has a genuinely small, well-known-constrained number of hardware FIFOs, and combining bulk endpoints (mass storage needs an IN+OUT pair) with the two HID interrupt endpoints may be exceeding what it can cleanly service, independent of LUN content. Two things worth checking:

1. **FIFO size tuning** — check if `dwc2` exposes anything here (different from the "speed" search that came up empty):

2. **Drop to one HID function + mass storage** — since mouse doesn't work on Linux targets anyway right now, temporarily removing *just* the mouse function (keep keyboard + storage) is both a clean diagnostic (does freeing up one interrupt endpoint's FIFO share let storage work?) *and* potentially just... the actual answer you need, since you said keyboard is the one you truly require for installers.
