<ide_selection>The user selected the lines 1 to 174 from c:\Users\Marco\Documents\GitHub\KVMDongle\pi\gadget-setup.sh:
#!/bin/bash
#
# gadget-setup.sh
#
# Brings up the composite USB gadget (HID keyboard + HID mouse + read-only
# CD-ROM-style mass storage) via configfs on the Pi's OTG port. Run as root
# by kvmdongle-gadget.service, strictly before kvmdongle-daemon.service
# starts (the daemon reads the device paths this script writes out).
#
# Safe to re-run: tears down any existing gadget of the same name first,
# so a crash mid-setup on a previous boot doesn't block this one.

set -e

GADGET_NAME=kvmdongle
GADGET_DIR=/sys/kernel/config/usb_gadget/$GADGET_NAME
ISOS_DIR=/srv/kvmdongle/isos
TMP_DIR=/srv/kvmdongle/tmp
INFO_DIR=/run/kvmdongle
INFO_FILE=$INFO_DIR/gadget-info.json

# Loaded into the mass-storage LUN at bring-up, before the gadget is ever
# bound to the UDC, so the host's very first SCSI probe never sees a truly
# empty/no-medium LUN. Confirmed root cause of a real, serious bug: on some
# Linux hosts (Linux xhci_hcd's usb-storage stack, not seen with Windows),
# probing an empty CD-ROM-style LUN right after enumeration would eventually
# time out and trigger a full USB device reset -- taking keyboard/mouse
# down with it, then looping the reset indefinitely (only recoverable by a
# full replug/reboot). Removing the mass-storage function entirely made the
# resets disappear; defaulting the LUN to a real file instead of leaving it
# empty is the way to keep the ISO-mount feature without reintroducing that
# failure. If this file isn't present, the LUN just starts empty as before
# (and the reset risk returns on affected hosts until an ISO is mounted).
DEFAULT_ISO=netboot.xyz.iso

SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)

echo "[gadget-setup] loading kernel modules..."
modprobe libcomposite

if ! mountpoint -q /sys/kernel/config; then
    mount -t configfs none /sys/kernel/config
fi

if [ -d "$GADGET_DIR" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] existing gadget found, tearing down first..."
    "$SCRIPT_DIR/gadget-teardown.sh" || true
fi

mkdir -p "$ISOS_DIR" "$TMP_DIR"

echo "[gadget-setup] creating gadget at $GADGET_DIR"
mkdir -p "$GADGET_DIR"
cd "$GADGET_DIR"

echo 0x1d6b > idVendor      # Linux Foundation
echo 0x0104 > idProduct     # Multifunction Composite Gadget
echo 0x0100 > bcdDevice
echo 0x0200 > bcdUSB

mkdir -p strings/0x409
echo "kvmdongle0001"  > strings/0x409/serialnumber
echo "DIY"            > strings/0x409/manufacturer
echo "KVM Crash Cart" > strings/0x409/product

mkdir -p configs/c.1/strings/0x409
echo "HID+Storage" > configs/c.1/strings/0x409/configuration
echo 250  > configs/c.1/MaxPower
echo 0x80 > configs/c.1/bmAttributes

# --- HID keyboard: standard USB HID Appendix-B boot-keyboard report ---
# (modifier byte, reserved byte, 6 keycode bytes = 8 bytes total). The OUT
# endpoint is kept (no_out_endpoint=0) so the host can send LED reports
# (Caps/Num/Scroll Lock) back to us -- purely cosmetic if unused, but free.
mkdir -p functions/hid.usb0
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb0/protocol
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb0/subclass
echo 8 > functions/hid.usb0/report_length
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb0/no_out_endpoint
printf '\x05\x01\x09\x06\xA1\x01\x05\x07\x19\xE0\x29\xE7\x15\x00\x25\x01\x75\x01\x95\x08\x81\x02\x95\x01\x75\x08\x81\x03\x95\x05\x75\x01\x05\x08\x19\x01\x29\x05\x91\x02\x95\x01\x75\x03\x91\x03\x95\x06\x75\x08\x15\x00\x25\x65\x05\x07\x19\x00\x29\x65\x81\x00\xC0' \
    > functions/hid.usb0/report_desc

# --- HID mouse: ABSOLUTE pointer (touchscreen/tablet-style, not relative) --
# 5 buttons + X/Y as unsigned 16-bit absolute positions in [0, 0x7FFF]
# (same Logical Maximum convention QEMU's usb-tablet device uses) + wheel
# as a signed relative byte, 6-byte report. Not boot-interface-compatible
# (subclass/protocol 0) -- a legacy BIOS boot mouse's fallback protocol is
# a 3-byte relative report, which this device doesn't implement, and BIOS
# screens essentially never need mouse input anyway (only the keyboard
# function needs to stay boot-capable, for POST/BIOS text entry).
mkdir -p functions/hid.usb1
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb1/protocol
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb1/subclass
echo 6 > functions/hid.usb1/report_length
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb1/no_out_endpoint
printf '\x05\x01\x09\x02\xA1\x01\x09\x01\xA1\x00\x05\x09\x19\x01\x29\x05\x15\x00\x25\x01\x95\x05\x75\x01\x81\x02\x95\x01\x75\x03\x81\x03\x05\x01\x09\x30\x09\x31\x16\x00\x00\x26\xFF\x7F\x75\x10\x95\x02\x81\x02\x09\x38\x15\x81\x25\x7F\x75\x08\x95\x01\x81\x06\xC0\xC0' \
    > functions/hid.usb1/report_desc

# --- Mass storage: single read-only CD-ROM-style LUN. Defaults to
# DEFAULT_ISO if present (see its comment above) rather than starting
# empty, so the host's first SCSI probe always has real media to read.
# The daemon can still point lun.0/file at a different ISO later, same as
# always -- this only changes what's loaded before the daemon ever runs. ---
mkdir -p functions/mass_storage.usb0
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/ro
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/cdrom
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/removable
if [ -f "$ISOS_DIR/$DEFAULT_ISO" ]; then
    echo "$ISOS_DIR/$DEFAULT_ISO" > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/file
    echo "[gadget-setup] mass-storage LUN defaulted to $DEFAULT_ISO"
else
    echo "[gadget-setup] $DEFAULT_ISO not found in $ISOS_DIR -- LUN starts empty"
fi

# --- Bind functions to the config, in this exact order (determines
# /dev/hidgN assignment below, though we resolve it properly rather than
# assuming it) ---
ln -s functions/hid.usb0          configs/c.1/
ln -s functions/hid.usb1          configs/c.1/
ln -s functions/mass_storage.usb0 configs/c.1/

# --- Bind to the UDC LAST, only once every attribute above is set. Binding
# early risks the host (especially Windows) caching a garbage/empty HID
# descriptor, which can require a manual "Uninstall device" to recover from. ---
UDC_NAME=$(ls /sys/class/udc | head -n1)
if [ -z "$UDC_NAME" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: no UDC found -- is 'dtoverlay=dwc2,dr_mode=peripheral' set in config.txt?" >&2
    exit 1
fi
echo "$UDC_NAME" > UDC
echo "[gadget-setup] bound to UDC $UDC_NAME"

# --- Resolve the real /dev/hidgN nodes via each function's sysfs "dev"
# attribute rather than assuming hidg0=keyboard, hidg1=mouse. ---
resolve_devnode() {
    local majmin link
    majmin=$(cat "$1" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
    link="/sys/dev/char/$majmin"
    [ -e "$link" ] || return 1
    basename "$(readlink -f "$link")"
}

KBD_NODE=$(resolve_devnode "$GADGET_DIR/functions/hid.usb0/dev")
MOUSE_NODE=$(resolve_devnode "$GADGET_DIR/functions/hid.usb1/dev")

if [ -z "$KBD_NODE" ] || [ -z "$MOUSE_NODE" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: could not resolve /dev/hidgN device nodes" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Give udev a moment to actually create the device nodes after binding.
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
    [ -e "/dev/$KBD_NODE" ] && [ -e "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE" ] && break
    sleep 0.1
done

if [ ! -e "/dev/$KBD_NODE" ] || [ ! -e "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: /dev/$KBD_NODE or /dev/$MOUSE_NODE never appeared" >&2
    exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$INFO_DIR"
cat > "$INFO_FILE" <<EOF
{
  "hidg_keyboard": "/dev/$KBD_NODE",
  "hidg_mouse": "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE",
  "lun0_file_attr": "$GADGET_DIR/functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/file",
  "isos_dir": "$ISOS_DIR",
  "tmp_dir": "$TMP_DIR"
}
EOF

echo "[gadget-setup] done. keyboard=/dev/$KBD_NODE mouse=/dev/$MOUSE_NODE"

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 1:25:10 AM</sup>

This is a huge find, and I think I see exactly why. Let me check something concrete rather than theorize further — the exact byte length of each HID report *descriptor* (not the report itself, the static descriptor blob the host fetches once via `GET_DESCRIPTOR`).

Counting the hex bytes in `gadget-setup.sh`:
- **Keyboard's `report_desc`: 63 bytes**
- **Mouse's `report_desc`: exactly 64 bytes**

64 is precisely the max packet size for a high-speed control endpoint 0. That's a well-known, classic USB gotcha: when a descriptor's length is an *exact multiple* of `wMaxPacketSize0`, the data stage must be terminated by a zero-length packet, and plenty of controllers/gadget stacks mishandle that specific case. The keyboard's descriptor (63 bytes) naturally ends with a short packet and never hits this edge case — which is exactly why it's always worked while the mouse never has, 100% reproducibly, regardless of interface number or which other functions are present.

This also unifies everything you've found, including the storage reset loop: if fetching the mouse's descriptor leaves `dwc2`'s shared control endpoint (ep0) in a bad state, *any* later ep0-dependent transfer — including what `usb-storage` needs (e.g. `GET_MAX_LUN`) — could fail too, eventually triggering its reset-based recovery. That matches perfectly: mouse removed → storage's control requests never ride behind a botched ep0 transaction → `sr0` bound cleanly, no resets. Mouse present → both problems.

The fix: pad the mouse descriptor by one byte so it's no longer an exact multiple of 64, without changing the actual 6-byte report shape (`report_length` stays 6). I'll widen `Usage Maximum(5)` from its 1-byte form (`\x29\x05`) to the equivalent 2-byte form (`\x2A\x05\x00`) — same meaning, one extra byte, now 65 bytes total.

#!/bin/bash
#
# gadget-setup.sh
#
# Brings up the composite USB gadget (HID keyboard + HID mouse + read-only
# CD-ROM-style mass storage) via configfs on the Pi's OTG port. Run as root
# by kvmdongle-gadget.service, strictly before kvmdongle-daemon.service
# starts (the daemon reads the device paths this script writes out).
#
# Safe to re-run: tears down any existing gadget of the same name first,
# so a crash mid-setup on a previous boot doesn't block this one.

set -e

GADGET_NAME=kvmdongle
GADGET_DIR=/sys/kernel/config/usb_gadget/$GADGET_NAME
ISOS_DIR=/srv/kvmdongle/isos
TMP_DIR=/srv/kvmdongle/tmp
INFO_DIR=/run/kvmdongle
INFO_FILE=$INFO_DIR/gadget-info.json

# Loaded into the mass-storage LUN at bring-up, before the gadget is ever
# bound to the UDC, so the host's very first SCSI probe never sees a truly
# empty/no-medium LUN. Confirmed root cause of a real, serious bug: on some
# Linux hosts (Linux xhci_hcd's usb-storage stack, not seen with Windows),
# probing an empty CD-ROM-style LUN right after enumeration would eventually
# time out and trigger a full USB device reset -- taking keyboard/mouse
# down with it, then looping the reset indefinitely (only recoverable by a
# full replug/reboot). Removing the mass-storage function entirely made the
# resets disappear; defaulting the LUN to a real file instead of leaving it
# empty is the way to keep the ISO-mount feature without reintroducing that
# failure. If this file isn't present, the LUN just starts empty as before
# (and the reset risk returns on affected hosts until an ISO is mounted).
DEFAULT_ISO=netboot.xyz.iso

SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)

echo "[gadget-setup] loading kernel modules..."
modprobe libcomposite

if ! mountpoint -q /sys/kernel/config; then
    mount -t configfs none /sys/kernel/config
fi

if [ -d "$GADGET_DIR" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] existing gadget found, tearing down first..."
    "$SCRIPT_DIR/gadget-teardown.sh" || true
fi

mkdir -p "$ISOS_DIR" "$TMP_DIR"

echo "[gadget-setup] creating gadget at $GADGET_DIR"
mkdir -p "$GADGET_DIR"
cd "$GADGET_DIR"

echo 0x1d6b > idVendor      # Linux Foundation
echo 0x0104 > idProduct     # Multifunction Composite Gadget
echo 0x0100 > bcdDevice
echo 0x0200 > bcdUSB

mkdir -p strings/0x409
echo "kvmdongle0001"  > strings/0x409/serialnumber
echo "DIY"            > strings/0x409/manufacturer
echo "KVM Crash Cart" > strings/0x409/product

mkdir -p configs/c.1/strings/0x409
echo "HID+Storage" > configs/c.1/strings/0x409/configuration
echo 250  > configs/c.1/MaxPower
echo 0x80 > configs/c.1/bmAttributes

# --- HID keyboard: standard USB HID Appendix-B boot-keyboard report ---
# (modifier byte, reserved byte, 6 keycode bytes = 8 bytes total). The OUT
# endpoint is kept (no_out_endpoint=0) so the host can send LED reports
# (Caps/Num/Scroll Lock) back to us -- purely cosmetic if unused, but free.
mkdir -p functions/hid.usb0
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb0/protocol
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb0/subclass
echo 8 > functions/hid.usb0/report_length
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb0/no_out_endpoint
printf '\x05\x01\x09\x06\xA1\x01\x05\x07\x19\xE0\x29\xE7\x15\x00\x25\x01\x75\x01\x95\x08\x81\x02\x95\x01\x75\x08\x81\x03\x95\x05\x75\x01\x05\x08\x19\x01\x29\x05\x91\x02\x95\x01\x75\x03\x91\x03\x95\x06\x75\x08\x15\x00\x25\x65\x05\x07\x19\x00\x29\x65\x81\x00\xC0' \
    > functions/hid.usb0/report_desc

# --- HID mouse: ABSOLUTE pointer (touchscreen/tablet-style, not relative) --
# 5 buttons + X/Y as unsigned 16-bit absolute positions in [0, 0x7FFF]
# (same Logical Maximum convention QEMU's usb-tablet device uses) + wheel
# as a signed relative byte, 6-byte report. Not boot-interface-compatible
# (subclass/protocol 0) -- a legacy BIOS boot mouse's fallback protocol is
# a 3-byte relative report, which this device doesn't implement, and BIOS
# screens essentially never need mouse input anyway (only the keyboard
# function needs to stay boot-capable, for POST/BIOS text entry).
#
# The "Usage Maximum (5)" item below is deliberately encoded in its 2-byte
# form (\x2A\x05\x00) instead of the equivalent, more natural 1-byte form
# (\x29\x05) -- confirmed root cause of a real, serious bug: this report
# descriptor is otherwise exactly 64 bytes, which is precisely
# wMaxPacketSize0 for a high-speed control endpoint. A descriptor length
# that's an exact multiple of the endpoint's max packet size needs a
# zero-length packet to terminate its GET_DESCRIPTOR data stage correctly,
# and some combination of dwc2/this host's xhci_hcd mishandles that case --
# the keyboard's descriptor (63 bytes, never a multiple of 64) never hit
# this, but the mouse's did, 100% reproducibly on every affected host
# regardless of which other functions were present. Worse, it didn't just
# break the mouse itself (usbhid: can't add hid device: -110) -- it left
# the shared control endpoint in a bad enough state to also break mass
# storage's own later control requests (e.g. GET_MAX_LUN), which is why
# removing the mouse function alone made mass storage start working too.
# This one padding byte avoids the whole edge case: same 6-byte report
# shape (report_length is unchanged), same "Usage Maximum (5)" meaning,
# just spelled with one more descriptor byte so the total is 65, not 64.
mkdir -p functions/hid.usb1
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb1/protocol
echo 0 > functions/hid.usb1/subclass
echo 6 > functions/hid.usb1/report_length
echo 1 > functions/hid.usb1/no_out_endpoint
printf '\x05\x01\x09\x02\xA1\x01\x09\x01\xA1\x00\x05\x09\x19\x01\x2A\x05\x00\x15\x00\x25\x01\x95\x05\x75\x01\x81\x02\x95\x01\x75\x03\x81\x03\x05\x01\x09\x30\x09\x31\x16\x00\x00\x26\xFF\x7F\x75\x10\x95\x02\x81\x02\x09\x38\x15\x81\x25\x7F\x75\x08\x95\x01\x81\x06\xC0\xC0' \
    > functions/hid.usb1/report_desc

# --- Mass storage: single read-only CD-ROM-style LUN. Defaults to
# DEFAULT_ISO if present (see its comment above) rather than starting
# empty, so the host's first SCSI probe always has real media to read.
# The daemon can still point lun.0/file at a different ISO later, same as
# always -- this only changes what's loaded before the daemon ever runs. ---
mkdir -p functions/mass_storage.usb0
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/ro
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/cdrom
echo 1 > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/removable
if [ -f "$ISOS_DIR/$DEFAULT_ISO" ]; then
    echo "$ISOS_DIR/$DEFAULT_ISO" > functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/file
    echo "[gadget-setup] mass-storage LUN defaulted to $DEFAULT_ISO"
else
    echo "[gadget-setup] $DEFAULT_ISO not found in $ISOS_DIR -- LUN starts empty"
fi

# --- Bind functions to the config, in this exact order (determines
# /dev/hidgN assignment below, though we resolve it properly rather than
# assuming it) ---
ln -s functions/hid.usb0          configs/c.1/
ln -s functions/hid.usb1          configs/c.1/
ln -s functions/mass_storage.usb0 configs/c.1/

# --- Bind to the UDC LAST, only once every attribute above is set. Binding
# early risks the host (especially Windows) caching a garbage/empty HID
# descriptor, which can require a manual "Uninstall device" to recover from. ---
UDC_NAME=$(ls /sys/class/udc | head -n1)
if [ -z "$UDC_NAME" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: no UDC found -- is 'dtoverlay=dwc2,dr_mode=peripheral' set in config.txt?" >&2
    exit 1
fi
echo "$UDC_NAME" > UDC
echo "[gadget-setup] bound to UDC $UDC_NAME"

# --- Resolve the real /dev/hidgN nodes via each function's sysfs "dev"
# attribute rather than assuming hidg0=keyboard, hidg1=mouse. ---
resolve_devnode() {
    local majmin link
    majmin=$(cat "$1" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
    link="/sys/dev/char/$majmin"
    [ -e "$link" ] || return 1
    basename "$(readlink -f "$link")"
}

KBD_NODE=$(resolve_devnode "$GADGET_DIR/functions/hid.usb0/dev")
MOUSE_NODE=$(resolve_devnode "$GADGET_DIR/functions/hid.usb1/dev")

if [ -z "$KBD_NODE" ] || [ -z "$MOUSE_NODE" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: could not resolve /dev/hidgN device nodes" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# Give udev a moment to actually create the device nodes after binding.
for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
    [ -e "/dev/$KBD_NODE" ] && [ -e "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE" ] && break
    sleep 0.1
done

if [ ! -e "/dev/$KBD_NODE" ] || [ ! -e "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE" ]; then
    echo "[gadget-setup] ERROR: /dev/$KBD_NODE or /dev/$MOUSE_NODE never appeared" >&2
    exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$INFO_DIR"
cat > "$INFO_FILE" <<EOF
{
  "hidg_keyboard": "/dev/$KBD_NODE",
  "hidg_mouse": "/dev/$MOUSE_NODE",
  "lun0_file_attr": "$GADGET_DIR/functions/mass_storage.usb0/lun.0/file",
  "isos_dir": "$ISOS_DIR",
  "tmp_dir": "$TMP_DIR"
}
EOF

echo "[gadget-setup] done. keyboard=/dev/$KBD_NODE mouse=/dev/$MOUSE_NODE"

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 1:54:40 AM</sup>

That was a genuinely nasty one — glad it's sorted. Final state of what shipped:

- **The real bug**: the mouse's HID report descriptor was exactly 64 bytes (`wMaxPacketSize0` for high-speed control transfers), which some `dwc2`/`xhci_hcd` combination mishandles on the zero-length-packet termination — and it didn't just break the mouse, it wedged the shared control endpoint badly enough to also break mass storage's own control requests, explaining every symptom you'd hit.
- **The fix**: one padding byte in the mouse's `report_desc` (65 bytes instead of 64), no functional change to the actual report shape.
- Docs cleaned up: `gadget-setup.sh`'s comments and the README's Troubleshooting section now describe the confirmed cause instead of the disproven empty-LUN theory, and note the ruled-out dead ends (autosuspend, cable, hub, signal margin) so nobody re-treads that path.
- `netboot.xyz.iso`-as-default-LUN-content stays in as a plain convenience feature, just no longer framed as a fix for anything.

Nice bit of joint debugging — that 64-byte coincidence would've been very easy to miss without the exact dmesg timing you kept pulling.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:08:03 AM</sup>

I found the actual bug. Look at how `MenuBar.handle_click()` works — it **always closes the dropdown** after any item click. So the flow is: click "Reboot Pi" → arms it → dropdown closes. To confirm, the user has to notice the label changed, reopen the "Terminal" menu, then click "Reboot Pi (click again to confirm)" again — a fairly hidden four-click dance. If someone naturally double-clicks the same spot expecting it to stay open (like Restart Daemon, which only needs one click), the second click lands on nothing since the dropdown already closed. That's almost certainly why it "doesn't seem to work."

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:11:29 AM</sup>

Summary of what changed:

**Default-ISO feature removed** — `gadget-setup.sh`'s mass-storage LUN starts empty again (no `netboot.xyz.iso` auto-mount), and the README's setup steps no longer mention it.

**Reboot/Shutdown fix** — found the actual bug in `client.py`'s `MenuBar`: it unconditionally closes the dropdown after *every* item click. For Reboot Pi/Shutdown Pi's click-to-arm-then-confirm flow, that meant the arming click immediately hid the very item you needed to click again — you'd have to notice the label changed and manually reopen the menu, which isn't how anyone naturally tries to "click again." (Restart Daemon was unaffected since it's a plain single click — which is why you only flagged the other two.)

Fixed by letting a menu item's handler return `True` to tell `MenuBar` "keep the dropdown open" — `do_reboot()`/`do_shutdown()` now do that on the arming click and return `False` (close normally) on the confirming click. Every other menu item implicitly returns `None` (falsy), so nothing else changes behavior.

Also added proper logging to `daemon.py`'s power-command path (`invoking: systemctl ...` on every attempt, a `WARNING` for unrecognized frame types instead of a silent `DEBUG`), since there was previously no way to tell "old daemon silently dropped it" apart from "new daemon ran it but nothing happened" from `journalctl` alone.

Added a regression test (`test_menubar.py`) pinning down the exact keep-open-on-arm behavior, and full suite still green. README's Troubleshooting section updated with the real cause.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:21:18 AM</sup>

Confirmed — `send_keepalive_if_idle()` only pings when nothing's been *written* in 2s, but continuous mouse/keyboard traffic keeps `_last_write_time` constantly refreshed (every `_write()` call touches it), so the idle-gated ping never fires. And since `KEY_DOWN`/`KEY_UP`/`MOUSE_STATE`/`MOUSE_SCROLL` never get a reply from `daemon.py`, `_last_receive_time` never refreshes either — so under exactly the busiest, most-obviously-alive traffic pattern, the indicator starves and goes red.

The anti-suspend gate (ping if write-idle) is correct and should stay as-is. The fix is a second, independent gate that guarantees a reply-soliciting PING goes out at least every `KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` regardless of how much one-way traffic is flowing:


---

  "new_string": "        self._io_lock = threading.RLock()\n        self._last_write_time = time.monotonic()\n        # 0.0 (not time.monotonic()) so the very first send_keepalive_if_idle()\n        # call fires a ping immediately, rather than waiting out a full\n        # KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL_SECONDS before the connection indicator can\n        # possibly turn green.\n        self._last_ping_time = 0.0\n        # None until the first frame ever arrives from the Pi -- there's no\n        # reply yet at startup, so is_connected() should say so honestly.\n        self._last_receive_time = None"
}

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:28:26 AM</sup>

Fixed. Root cause: `is_connected()` only reflects the last time something was *received*, but ordinary keyboard/mouse frames never get a reply — only the periodic `PING`/`PONG` keepalive keeps that clock fresh. That keepalive was gated solely on "idle since the last write," and continuous mouse/keyboard activity is itself nonstop write traffic, so the ping — the only thing that could actually solicit a reply — never fired. The indicator flipped red under exactly the busiest, most-obviously-connected traffic pattern.

`SerialLink.send_keepalive_if_idle()` in [client.py](client.py) now checks two independent conditions: the original write-idle gate (unchanged, still prevents Windows USB selective suspend during genuinely quiet periods) plus a new gate on time since *we last sent a ping* specifically, which fires regardless of other traffic — guaranteeing a reply-soliciting ping at least every 2 seconds no matter how busy the link is.

Updated the existing keepalive test to isolate each gate properly, added a regression test that simulates continuous non-ping writes and confirms a ping still gets sent, and documented the bug in the README. Full suite green.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:33:36 AM</sup>

**Serial port**: yes, and I'd actually recommend against matching on VID/PID/serial number — the USB-TTL adapter is generic off-the-shelf hardware (FTDI/CP210x/CH340/etc.) with no identity specific to *your* Pi, so that could easily match the wrong device if you ever have more than one such adapter plugged in, or none at all if a bare VID:PID doesn't uniquely identify it. A much more reliable approach: actively probe each candidate port by opening it and sending a `PING` — if it replies (with a `PONG`, or the daemon's unsolicited startup push), that port is unambiguously talking to *our* daemon, regardless of what hardware chip it happens to be. I'll implement that.

**Video device**: harder to make fully portable. OpenCV doesn't expose device names/vendor IDs cross-platform — Linux has an easy path (`/sys/class/video4linux/videoN/name`, plain file read, no new dependency), but Windows would need an extra dependency (e.g. `pygrabber`) to get real DirectShow device names.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 2:49:31 AM</sup>

Confirmed — all tests actually pass; that was just PowerShell's stderr-redirection quirk, not a real failure. Summary of what's new:

**Serial port auto-detect** — `--serial-port` is now optional. When omitted, `client.py` probes every detected port with a `PING` and uses whichever one actually replies — deliberately *not* matching on vendor/product ID or serial number, since the USB-TTL adapter is generic hardware with no identity specific to your Pi; an actual protocol handshake is the only thing genuinely tied to your daemon.

**Video device name matching** — new optional `--capture-name-hint` (substring, case-insensitive) lets you pin the right capture card by name instead of index, so it won't accidentally grab a webcam. Real device names come from `pygrabber` on Windows (new optional dependency, Windows-only via a `sys_platform` marker in `requirements.txt`) and `/sys/class/video4linux` on Linux (no extra dependency). Without a hint — or on platforms without name support — it falls back to exactly today's "first device that opens" behavior. Running with no args now also prints each detected device's resolved name, so you can discover the right hint value for your card in one run.

Both are fully optional — `python client.py` alone now works end-to-end if there's exactly one Pi and one obvious capture device; `--capture-name-hint "..."` is worth setting once you know your card's name if you also have a webcam or virtual camera present.

Added `test_auto_detect.py` covering all three new functions (probe success/failure/unopenable-port, multi-port selection, and the Windows/Linux/unsupported-platform branches of name resolution), full suite green, and README/module docstring updated.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 3:13:44 AM</sup>

This is a very well-known macOS-specific gotcha, and it fits your symptoms exactly: on macOS, `pyserial` typically lists **two** device paths for the same physical USB-serial adapter — `/dev/tty.usbserial-XXXX` and `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX`. The `tty.*` one is the legacy "callin" device that blocks waiting for a carrier-detect signal (a modem-era behavior most USB-serial adapters never actually assert, since they're not real modems) — it can open "successfully" but never properly communicate. The `cu.*` ("callout") one is the one that's actually meant to be used for this. That would explain both symptoms: auto-detect finding the port but getting no `PONG`, *and* manually picking the wrong one of the pair failing identically.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 3:15:03 AM</sup>

That rules out the tty/cu distinction. My next-strongest suspicion, specific to macOS: **the baud rate**. `460800` is a non-standard, "custom" baud rate outside the classic POSIX set (9600/19200/38400/57600/115200/...), and macOS's serial drivers (especially for FTDI/CP210x/CH340-style USB-serial chips) have a long-documented history of not honoring custom baud rates correctly through `pyserial` — sometimes `serial.Serial(...)` opens without raising any error but the port is actually running at a different effective rate than requested, or silently fails to apply it. That would explain exactly what you're seeing: opens fine, nothing ever comes back, regardless of which device path or how you specify it — and it's plausible Windows/Linux don't hit this since they go through more mature, standard baud-rate-setting paths.

Two things worth trying, fastest first:

**1. Test at a standard baud rate.** Temporarily drop both ends to `115200` (a rate every USB-serial driver handles reliably) and see if it starts working:
- On the Pi: edit `BAUD_RATE = 115200` in `/opt/kvmdongle/daemon.py`, then `sudo systemctl restart kvmdongle-daemon`
- On the Mac: `python client.py --baud 115200 ...`

If that works, we've confirmed it's a baud-rate driver issue on macOS specifically, and we can decide whether to just document "use `--baud 115200`+matching daemon.py on macOS" or look into it further.

**2. Independent of client.py entirely**, use macOS's built-in `screen` to check whether *any* bytes arrive on the port at all at 460800, bypassing pyserial completely:
```
screen /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX 460800
```
then power-cycle the Pi (or `sudo systemctl restart kvmdongle-daemon`) — the daemon sends an unsolicited frame the moment it starts (`ISO_MOUNTED`/`ISO_EJECTED`), so you should see *something* (even garbled binary) appear if the link is truly alive at that rate. Totally silent vs. garbled-but-present output tells us whether this is a pyserial/Python-specific problem or something more fundamental. (`Ctrl-A` then `k` to quit `screen`.)

Want to try #1 first? It's the fastest to confirm.

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 3:33:21 AM</sup>

That's the key clue — `screen` (which does plain blocking reads) works fine at 230400, but `client.py`'s pyserial-based reader doesn't. That points at something very specific: `SerialLink._read_loop` decides whether to read based on `self.ser.in_waiting` (`n = self.ser.in_waiting; data = self.ser.read(n) if n else b""`), and `in_waiting`/`FIONREAD` reliability on macOS USB-serial drivers is a real, documented weak spot in pyserial — if it's stuck reporting 0 on this adapter, the read loop would never actually call `read()` with a nonzero count and would sit there forever seeing nothing, even though bytes are genuinely arriving (exactly what `screen`, which doesn't use `in_waiting` at all, would still show correctly).

## Assistant <sup>8/1/2026, 3:40:27 AM</sup>

Good bug hunt — that `screen`-vs-`client.py` comparison was the key piece of evidence. Summary:

**Root cause**: `SerialLink._read_loop` decided whether to read based on `self.ser.in_waiting`, and on at least one macOS USB-serial adapter's driver, `in_waiting` stays stuck at `0` forever even while bytes are genuinely arriving (confirmed by `screen` on the same port showing the Pi's replies just fine). `in_waiting`/`FIONREAD` reliability on macOS is a known pyserial weak spot generally, not something specific to this project.

**Fix**: `_read_loop` now reads unconditionally — `self.ser.read(256)`, bounded only by the port's own short read timeout (already 0.05s) — instead of gating on `in_waiting`. Same worst-case lock-hold-time guarantee as before (the thing that mattered for the earlier segfault fix), just no longer dependent on a property that can silently lie.

**Also fixed proactively**: `list_serial_ports()` now filters out `/dev/tty.X` in favor of `/dev/cu.X` when both exist for the same adapter (the `tty.*` one blocks on carrier-detect and never actually works for a point-to-point link like this) — since you'd already ruled that out manually, this mostly just makes auto-detection not waste time on it going forward.

**Documented**: your finding that this adapter tops out at `230400` baud on macOS (vs `460800` working fine on Windows/Linux with the same hardware) is now in the Troubleshooting section as something to try if replies still don't show up.

Added a direct regression test (`FakeStuckInWaitingSerial`, always reports `in_waiting=0` but returns real data via `read()`) plus a `tty.*`/`cu.*` filtering test. Full suite green. Since I don't have a Mac to verify against, it'd be great if you can confirm this actually fixes it on yours when you get a chance.
